stem: A nurse is reviewing a patient’s file before surgery and notices that the allergy history is not documented. According to the surgical safety checklist, at which stage should allergies be confirmed?
why_right: In the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, Sign In is done before induction of anesthesia and includes confirming identity, site, procedure and consent, the site marking, the anesthesia safety check, pulse oximetry, and explicitly "Does the patient have a known allergy?", along with airway and blood-loss risk. Allergies must be known before any anesthetic agent or antibiotic is given, so they are confirmed at Sign In.
why_wrong_block:
B. Sign Out: done before the patient leaves the operating room; it covers the procedure name, instrument, sponge and needle counts, specimen labeling, equipment problems and recovery concerns.
C. Time Out: done before skin incision; the team introduces itself, reconfirms patient, site and procedure, antibiotic prophylaxis within the last 60 minutes, anticipated critical events and imaging. Allergy is checked earlier, before induction.
D. Postoperative: not a phase of the checklist, and too late; anesthetic drugs and antibiotics would already have been given.
key_concept:
WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: 3 phases.
  • Sign In (before induction): identity, site, consent, site marking, anesthesia check, oximeter, allergy, airway/aspiration risk, blood-loss risk
  • Time Out (before incision): team introductions, confirm patient/site/procedure, antibiotics within 60 min, critical events, imaging
  • Sign Out (before leaving OR): procedure recorded, counts, specimen labeling, equipment issues, recovery plan
exam_pearl: Allergy, airway and blood-loss risk = Sign In; antibiotics within 60 minutes = Time Out; counts and specimens = Sign Out.

stem: A 28 year old female presented following radiation of neck with neck swelling. Ultrasound showed swelling in the left lobe of the thyroid of 3x4cm of papillary thyroid cancer. Which of the following is the best management?
why_right: This is confirmed papillary thyroid cancer (3x4 cm) in a patient with a history of neck radiation. Prior head and neck irradiation raises the risk of multifocal and bilateral disease, and is a standard indication for total thyroidectomy rather than lobectomy, even for a tumor that would otherwise allow a lobectomy. Total thyroidectomy also allows radioactive iodine therapy and thyroglobulin surveillance afterwards.
why_wrong_block:
A. Left lobectomy: an option for low-risk, unifocal differentiated cancer (roughly 1 to 4 cm) without risk factors, or for an indeterminate Bethesda IV nodule; the radiation history removes this option.
B. Left lobectomy with isthmusectomy: still a unilateral procedure, with the same limitation as lobectomy; it leaves the contralateral lobe at risk in a radiation-exposed gland.
C. Subtotal thyroidectomy: leaves residual thyroid tissue, which is inadequate oncologically and interferes with radioactive iodine; it is an old operation for benign goiter or Graves disease.
key_concept:
Differentiated thyroid cancer: extent of surgery.
  • <1 cm, low risk: active surveillance or lobectomy
  • 1 to 4 cm, low risk: lobectomy or total thyroidectomy
  • >4 cm, extrathyroidal extension, nodal or distant metastases, prior radiation, bilateral nodules: total thyroidectomy
  • Bethesda VI (malignant): near-total / total thyroidectomy
  • Medullary cancer: total thyroidectomy
exam_pearl: History of neck irradiation pushes any thyroid cancer toward total thyroidectomy.

stem: An elderly man with a known history of BPH presents to OPD with difficult urination, frequency, urgency, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. He has been treated with an alpha-blocker for the past 2 years, with persistent symptoms. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptA: Adjust the dose of the alpha-blocker
highlight_terms_source: alpha-blocker for the past 2 years, with persistent symptoms
why_right: BPH is treated initially with an alpha-blocker, and TURP is the definitive treatment when medical therapy fails. Here the man has been on an alpha-blocker for 2 years with persistent symptoms (hesitancy, frequency, urgency, incomplete emptying), which is failure of medical therapy, so the most appropriate next step among these options is TURP.
why_wrong_block:
A. Adjust the alpha-blocker dose: alpha-blockers have a quick, largely dose-limited effect; after 2 years of persistent symptoms, a higher dose adds side effects (orthostatic hypotension) without meaningful benefit.
B. Suprapubic catheterization: used for acute retention when urethral catheterization fails or is contraindicated (e.g. urethral trauma or stricture); this patient is voiding, not in retention.
C. Clean intermittent catheterization: for neurogenic bladder or chronic retention in patients unfit for surgery; it is not the next step for symptomatic BPH failing medication.
key_concept:
BPH management ladder.
  • Initial: lifestyle measures + alpha-blocker (tamsulosin, doxazosin)
  • Large gland: add a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride)
  • Failed medical therapy or complications (retention, recurrent UTI, stones, hematuria, renal impairment): TURP
  • Very large gland: open or enucleation prostatectomy
  • Acute retention: Foley catheter + urine culture
exam_pearl: New LUTS with an enlarged prostate = alpha-blocker; persistent symptoms despite long medical treatment = TURP.

stem: A patient with spinal metastasis presents with rapidly progressive paraparesis and fecal incontinence (level T something). His symptoms continue to worsen despite medical management. What is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: rapidly progressive paraparesis and fecal incontinence
continue to worsen despite medical management
why_right: This is metastatic spinal cord compression with "rapidly progressive paraparesis" and sphincter loss ("fecal incontinence") that keeps worsening despite medical management (steroids). Progressive deficit despite steroids is the indication for urgent surgical decompression (usually with stabilization, followed by radiotherapy), which gives the best chance of preserving or regaining walking and continence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chemotherapy acts too slowly to relieve an acute compression; it is used only for very chemosensitive tumors alongside definitive local treatment.
B. Steroids are the first step to reduce cord edema, but they have already failed here; escalating them does not decompress the cord.
C. Conservative care would be right only for a patient unfit for surgery or with very poor prognosis; with a progressing deficit it risks permanent paraplegia.
key_concept:
Metastatic cord compression: steroids immediately, MRI whole spine, then decompress.
  • Red flags: back pain, leg weakness, sensory level, bladder/bowel dysfunction.
  • Immediate: high-dose dexamethasone.
  • Imaging: urgent MRI whole spine.
  • Progressive deficit, instability or failed medical therapy: urgent surgery then radiotherapy.
  • Unfit for surgery or radiosensitive tumor: radiotherapy.
exam_pearl: Worsening despite steroids is the trigger that turns the answer from radiotherapy/steroids to surgery.

stem: Pts in the 4th post op day complaining of fever only what is the best next ?
why_right: By the postoperative fever timeline, fever on days 4 to 5 points to surgical site (wound) infection or DVT. On the 4th post-op day with fever as the only complaint, the best next step is to examine the wound for redness, warmth, discharge or collection; if infection is found, the wound is opened and drained.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC: may support infection but does not localize the source; the decisive next step is the targeted bedside examination of the surgical site.
B. Urine culture: UTI is the classic cause on days 2 to 3 (especially after catheterization); on day 4 the wound comes first.
D. Review medication: drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion, considered later when no infectious source is found.
key_concept:
Post-operative fever by day.
  • Day 1: atelectasis (or early necrotizing wound infection)
  • Days 2 to 3: UTI, superficial thrombophlebitis, pneumonia
  • Days 4 to 5: surgical site infection, DVT
  • Day 6 and beyond: wound dehiscence, deep collection or abscess (CT)
  • SSI management: open the wound and drain; CT if deep infection suspected
exam_pearl: Day 3 fever pushes you to the urine; day 4 to 5 fever pushes you to the wound.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler note: It Was "Wound Exploration", Not "Wound Assessment".

stem: Patient presents with a warm, erythematous swelling of the thigh with indistinct borders, accompanied by lymphangitis, and regional lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A "warm, erythematous swelling" with "indistinct borders" is the classic description of cellulitis, an infection of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue usually caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus. Accompanying lymphangitis (red streaks) and regional lymphadenopathy show spread along lymphatics, which fits streptococcal cellulitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Necrotizing fasciitis shows pain out of proportion to findings, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, crepitus, bullae or skin necrosis; none are described here.
B. Folliculitis gives small pustules centred on hair follicles, not a diffuse warm swelling with lymphangitis.
D. Impetigo is a superficial epidermal infection with honey-coloured crusts, typically on the face of children.
key_concept:
Skin infection depth: impetigo (epidermis) → erysipelas (upper dermis, SHARP raised border) → cellulitis (deep dermis/subcutis, INDISTINCT border) → necrotizing fasciitis (fascia).
  • Cellulitis: oral anti-staphylococcal/streptococcal antibiotic; IV if systemic features
  • Fluctuant collection = abscess → drainage
  • Pain out of proportion, crepitus, toxicity → necrotizing fasciitis → urgent surgical debridement
exam_pearl: Sharp, raised, well-demarcated border flips the diagnosis to erysipelas.

stem: A 70-year-old female presents with a complaint of rectal pain and passing mucus. This exact picture was shown: What is the diagnosis?
why_right: The image shows circumferential, concentric mucosal folds protruding through the anus in a 70-year-old woman with mucus discharge and rectal discomfort. Full-thickness rectal prolapse is typical of elderly women (weak pelvic floor, chronic straining), and the exposed mucosa secretes mucus. Concentric rings indicate the whole rectal wall has prolapsed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Skin tag: a small, soft, skin-covered flap at the anal verge, often painless or linked to a fissure; it is not a mucosal, circumferential protrusion.
C. Haemorrhoid: prolapsed hemorrhoids appear as separate cushions with radial grooves between them, and classically present with painless bright red bleeding, not concentric circular folds.
key_concept:
Anal protrusion: read the folds.
  • Concentric (circular) folds: full-thickness rectal prolapse
  • Radial folds, separate cushions: prolapsed hemorrhoids or mucosal prolapse
  • Small skin-covered tag: skin tag (sentinel tag with a posterior fissure)
  • Rectal prolapse: elderly women, straining, mucus, incontinence
  • Treatment: surgical (perineal approach in frail elderly, abdominal rectopexy if fit)
exam_pearl: Concentric rings = rectal prolapse; radial grooves = hemorrhoids.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Photo shows circumferential concentric mucosal folds protruding from the anus.

stem: Patient in 60s diagnosed with prostate cancer presenting with back pain (and maybe lower limb weakness). What is the appropriate next step for him?
why_wrong_block:
A. IV hydrocortisone captures the steroid idea, but the steroid of choice for cord edema is dexamethasone, and steroid alone without urgent MRI leaves the level and cause of compression undefined.
B. MRI is the right test, but outpatient timing is wrong: suspected cord compression needs same-day imaging, because delay risks permanent paralysis and sphincter loss. Outpatient MRI suits chronic mechanical back pain without red flags.
key_concept:
Back pain in a patient with cancer = spinal cord compression until proven otherwise.
  • Commonest culprits: prostate, breast, lung (bone metastases to spine)
  • Immediate: high-dose IV dexamethasone
  • Imaging: urgent whole spine MRI (not outpatient)
  • Definitive: radiotherapy or surgical decompression after MRI
  • A normal neuro exam does not exclude impending compression
exam_pearl: Right idea, wrong detail: hydrocortisone instead of dexamethasone, or MRI booked outpatient, are both traps in a cancer patient with back pain.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Both options crossed out with pen X marks. Embedded AI note: suspected spinal cord compression (oncologic emergency); neither A nor B correct; correct: urgent (not outpatient) whole spine MRI and high-dose IV corticosteroids, typically dexamethasone not hydrocortisone. Outpatient MRI inappropriate given urgency.
Other marked answers: Screenshot Answer line: A (IV hydrocortisone)

stem: A young man was brought to the Emergency Department after he was hit in the chest while playing football. On examination, he was dyspneic and drowsy with GCS 11/15. Tracheal shifting to the left and raised JVP were noted. He has barely audible breath sounds on the right side. Blood pressure 80/50 mmHg Heart rate 130 /min Respiratory rate 32 /min Temperature 36.6 °C Oxygen saturation 90% Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: barely audible breath sounds on the right side
why_right: After a chest blow, this man has barely audible breath sounds on the right, trachea shifted to the left (away from the silent side), raised JVP and shock (BP 80/50, HR 130). That combination of unilateral silent chest, contralateral tracheal deviation, distended neck veins and hypotension is a right tension pneumothorax, an obstructive shock needing immediate decompression.
why_wrong_block:
A. Flail segment needs multiple rib fractures with paradoxical chest wall movement; it causes hypoxia and pain but does not shift the trachea or raise the JVP.
B. Cardiac tamponade also gives raised JVP and hypotension (Beck triad with muffled heart sounds), but breath sounds stay equal and the trachea stays central; it is typical of penetrating injury.
C. Pulmonary contusion causes hypoxia and crackles developing over hours, but no tracheal deviation, raised JVP or obstructive shock.
key_concept:
Raised JVP + hypotension after chest trauma: decide tension vs tamponade by the lungs and trachea.
  • Tension pneumothorax: silent hyperresonant side, trachea shifted away, raised JVP, shock
  • Tamponade: equal breath sounds, central trachea, muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus
  • Massive hemothorax: silent DULL side, flat neck veins
  • Flail chest: paradoxical segment, supportive care
  • Tension treatment: needle decompression then chest tube (clinical diagnosis, no X-ray first)
exam_pearl: Silent side + distended neck veins = tension; silent side + flat neck veins and dullness = massive hemothorax.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' variant: MVA with distended neck vein, trachea shifted to the other side, absent sound, hyperresonance on percussion, BP 80/60; options Cardiac tamponade / Massive hemithorax / Tension pneumothorax (highlighted, consistent).

stem: pt with night cough, itchy eye, palate, and nose, darkining of the eyelid:
key_concept:
Rhinitis types by history.
  • Allergic: itching (eyes, nose, palate), sneezing, clear discharge, shiners, seasonal or perennial triggers; treat with intranasal steroid, antihistamine, allergen avoidance
  • Rhinitis medicamentosa: rebound congestion after prolonged topical decongestant; treat by stopping the decongestant plus intranasal steroid
  • Infective: purulent discharge, fever
  • Vasomotor: triggered by temperature, odours, no itch
exam_pearl: Itch plus allergic shiners = allergic rhinitis; congestion only, with a decongestant spray history = rhinitis medicamentosa.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Screenshot recall (options remembered as 'Allergic rhinosinuitia / rhinitis medicamentosa something like that'). Second screenshot of same question: pediatric night cough and complaining of nasal discharge (clear), on examination dark periorbital; options were Rhinitis Medicamentosa / Allergic rhinitis. No answer marked.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A patient presents after a small wooden object entered his eye. He complains of severe eye pain, inability to open the eye, and photophobia. An eye examination was performed using fluorescein staining, which showed an epithelial injury or tear something like that What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: small wooden object entered his eye
why_right: Acute onset after a small object entered the eye, with severe pain, inability to open the eye and photophobia, and fluorescein uptake showing an epithelial defect is a corneal abrasion. Fluorescein stains areas where the corneal epithelium is missing, and a linear defect fits a scratch from the foreign body.
why_wrong_block:
A. A corneal ulcer (infective keratitis) develops over days, often in contact lens wearers, and shows a white infiltrate or opacity with a staining defect; this is an immediate traumatic defect.
C. Subconjunctival hemorrhage is painless with a bright red patch and no fluorescein uptake.
D. Acute conjunctivitis gives redness with discharge and grittiness, usually without severe pain or a staining epithelial defect.
key_concept:
Trauma + pain + photophobia + fluorescein uptake = corneal abrasion.
  • Evert lids to look for a retained foreign body (vertical linear abrasions)
  • Treat: topical antibiotic, analgesia; no steroid drops
  • Do not give topical anaesthetic to take home
  • Vegetable matter or contact lens: watch for infective keratitis
  • Opacity or infiltrate = ulcer, refer
exam_pearl: A white infiltrate over the staining area, or symptoms evolving over days, turns an abrasion into a corneal ulcer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' variant: cutting woods, felt something in eye, tearing, photosensitivity, cannot close the eye, normal visual acuity, fluorescein shows linear epithelial lesion; options corneal abrasion (highlighted) / corneal ulcer.

stem: Lesser sac 9 cm cyst posterior to the stomach
highlight_terms_source: 9 cm cyst posterior to the stomach
key_concept:
Lesser sac cyst behind the stomach: the history and cyst features decide pseudocyst versus neoplasm.
  • Pseudocyst: homogenous, thin wall, more than 4 weeks after pancreatitis; CT is the best imaging
  • Small, young or asymptomatic: observe; large, persistent or growing: endoscopic (internal) drainage
  • Fever, leukocytosis, gas or thick irregular wall: abscess or infected collection, percutaneous drainage
  • Septations, solid parts, no pancreatitis history: think cystic neoplasm
exam_pearl: Without a pancreatitis history and with septations or solid components, the same location points to a cystic neoplasm, not a pseudocyst.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 6 or 7 years old child fell and subsequently became drowsy, nauseated, and started vomiting. GCS is decreased but not ≤8 (I don't remember exactly) CT scan shows a crescent shaped intracranial bleeding. What is the best management?
why_right: After a fall, the child became drowsy, nauseated and vomiting with a reduced GCS, and CT shows a crescent-shaped bleed, which is a subdural hematoma (torn bridging veins). A symptomatic acute traumatic hematoma with neurological deterioration and raised intracranial pressure signs needs urgent neurosurgical evacuation to relieve mass effect. Because the GCS is not ≤8 and the airway is maintained, definitive decompression takes priority over intubation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Intubation is indicated for GCS ≤8, inability to protect the airway, hypoxia or aspiration risk; here the GCS is reduced but above 8, so the airway is not the immediate problem.
C. Reassurance fits a minor head injury with normal GCS and no imaging findings; a child with vomiting, drowsiness and an intracranial bleed on CT cannot be reassured.
D. CT already made the diagnosis and is the test of choice for acute head trauma; MRI only delays treatment and is reserved for subacute or subtle injuries (for example diffuse axonal injury).
key_concept:
Acute intracranial bleed on CT + deterioration = surgical evacuation.
  • Subdural: crescent (concave), bridging veins
  • Epidural: lens (biconvex), middle meningeal artery, lucid interval
  • CT without contrast is the first imaging in head trauma
  • Intubate if GCS ≤8 or airway not protected
  • Small, asymptomatic hematoma without shift: may be observed with serial CT
exam_pearl: If the stem gave GCS ≤8, airway first; with GCS above 8 and a symptomatic bleed, go to evacuation.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for pallor and easy fatigability since early childhood. He has no history of bleeding. On examination: mild splenomegaly. CBC: Hb = 8 g/dL; MCV = 62 fL; RBC count = normal to high. Peripheral blood smear shows numerous target cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: pallor and easy fatigability since early childhood
why_right: Pallor "since early childhood" with mild splenomegaly, a very low MCV (62) out of proportion to the anemia, a "normal to high" RBC count and "numerous target cells" is the thalassemia pattern. The marrow makes many small, poorly hemoglobinized cells (high RBC count, Mentzer index below 13), and chronic extravascular hemolysis enlarges the spleen. Hemoglobin electrophoresis (raised HbA2 and HbF) confirms beta thalassemia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Iron deficiency also causes microcytosis, but the RBC count falls with it (Mentzer above 13), target cells are not prominent and splenomegaly is not expected; in a child it usually follows a poor diet such as excess cow's milk, with low ferritin.
B. Anemia of chronic disease needs an underlying chronic illness, is usually normocytic or mildly microcytic, has high ferritin and no splenomegaly or target cells.
C. Sideroblastic anemia shows ringed sideroblasts on marrow and high iron; it is rare in children and has no high RBC count or prominent target cells.
key_concept:
Microcytic anemia: separate by RBC count, iron studies and electrophoresis.
  • Thalassemia: RBC count normal or high, Mentzer (MCV/RBC) below 13, target cells, raised HbA2.
  • Iron deficiency: low RBC count, Mentzer above 13, low ferritin, high RDW.
  • Chronic disease: high ferritin, low TIBC.
  • Sideroblastic: ringed sideroblasts, high iron.
  • Failure to respond to iron points to thalassemia.
exam_pearl: Very low MCV with a high RBC count is thalassemia until proven otherwise; iron deficiency drops the RBC count.

stem: A 23-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department after he fell down from 3 m height on his right leg. Examination revealed a deformity of the leg with an open wound in the mid-leg and devitalized tissue and dirt in the wound. The leg was put in a splint Blood pressure 112/70 mmhg Heart rate 99 /min Respiratory rate 22 /min Oxygen saturation 95 % Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: devitalized tissue and dirt in the wound
key_concept:
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Surgical debridement (antibiotics-first is argued as the alternative).
  • Open fracture sequence: IV antibiotics + tetanus, splint or reduce
  • Then urgent debridement and irrigation in theatre
  • Then definitive fixation: IM nail, or external fixator if soft tissues are badly damaged
  • Lead-in decides: first step in ED = antibiotics; surgical next step = debridement
exam_pearl: If the stem says antibiotics were already given, debridement is unequivocally next.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: BP printed as '11270 mmhg' (likely 112/70).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A patient with diabetes presents with swelling of the big toe and warmth and tenderness of the calf for 4 days. There is a 2-cm ulcer over the first metatarsal area. No discharge is noted. Distal pulses are intact. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
highlight_terms_source: warmth and tenderness of the calf
why_right: The decisive clues are warmth and tenderness of the calf for 4 days with limb swelling and intact distal pulses: arterial insufficiency is unlikely and deep vein thrombosis (or venous disease) must be excluded. Duplex ultrasound is the non-invasive, first-line test that assesses venous flow and thrombus (and can also assess arterial flow), so it is the most appropriate initial investigation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Conventional angiography is invasive arterial imaging used for intervention planning in established arterial disease; with intact pulses it is not an initial test.
C. ABI is the first test for suspected peripheral arterial disease (claudication, absent pulses, arterial ulcer); it does not detect DVT and is often falsely high in diabetics with calcified vessels.
D. CT with contrast (or CT angiography) suits acute limb ischemia or deep abscess or osteomyelitis planning; it is not the initial test for a warm tender calf and carries contrast risk in a diabetic.
key_concept:
Leg problem: check the pulses first, then pick the test.
  • Pulses intact + calf swelling, warmth, tenderness: duplex ultrasound for DVT
  • Pulses intact + gaiter ulcer: venous duplex
  • Absent pulses, claudication: ABI first, then arterial duplex, then CT angiography
  • Acute ischemia (sudden pain, absent pulses): CT angiography
exam_pearl: A diabetic foot ulcer is a distractor here; the warm tender calf with intact pulses makes it a venous question.

stem: Newborn didn't pass meconium for 48h when examining the rectum it exploded with temporarily relieve of the symptoms. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: Failure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours in a term newborn is the classic red flag for Hirschsprung disease. On rectal examination the stool and gas "exploded" out with temporary relief (the squirt or blast sign): the finger dilates the aganglionic, tight segment and releases the obstruction above it.
why_wrong_block: B. Functional constipation is a disease of older infants and children (often around toilet training) with a normal meconium history and a rectum full of hard stool; a newborn who has not passed meconium in 48 hours must be assumed to have an organic cause.
key_concept:
Delayed meconium (>24 to 48 h) + explosive stool after DRE = Hirschsprung.
  • DRE: tight sphincter, empty rectum, explosive release of stool and gas
  • Contrast enema: transition zone (narrow distal, dilated proximal)
  • Diagnosis: rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells
  • Association: Down syndrome
  • Alternatives in a neonate: meconium ileus (cystic fibrosis), meconium plug, hypothyroidism
exam_pearl: Normal meconium passage in the first 24 to 48 hours makes Hirschsprung much less likely; delayed meconium makes functional constipation the wrong answer.

stem: child with flu symptoms + trial of amoxicillin with no improvement. Mother asking about preventive measures?
why_right: "Flu symptoms" with no response to amoxicillin points to a viral respiratory infection, which antibiotics do not treat or prevent. The question asks about "preventive measures", and the evidence-based prevention for respiratory infections in children is immunisation (seasonal influenza vaccine, plus completing routine vaccines such as pneumococcal, Hib and pertussis), alongside hand hygiene.
why_wrong_block: A. Vitamin C supplements have not been shown to prevent colds or flu in the general population; at most they may modestly shorten symptom duration. It would only be right if the child had true scurvy (bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhage, poor diet).
key_concept:
Viral URTI: antibiotics do not help; prevention = vaccination + hygiene.
  • Annual influenza vaccine from 6 months of age
  • Complete routine schedule (pneumococcal, Hib, pertussis, measles)
  • Hand washing, avoid smoke exposure
  • Vitamin C: no proven preventive benefit
exam_pearl: Failure of amoxicillin is a clue that the illness is viral; the preventive answer is a vaccine, not a supplement or prophylactic antibiotic.

stem: Patient presents with depression, loss of appetite, start isolation from people, and want to use of marijuana to relieve stress . They also show anxiety and depression drug no compliance. (On examination she was Unkempt with slurred speech.) What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
why_right: She uses marijuana "to relieve stress", is unkempt with "slurred speech" and is not taking her psychiatric drugs, so substance intoxication or use must be excluded first. A urine drug screen is quick, cheap and directly tests the most likely contributor to her depressive picture and neurological sign. Substance use changes the diagnosis (substance induced mood disorder) and the management, so it is the most appropriate initial test.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC: useful when anemia or infection could explain fatigue, but nothing here points to it, and it does not explain slurred speech with cannabis use.
C. Pulmonary function test: would be relevant for chronic respiratory symptoms in a smoker, not for evaluating a mood and behaviour change.
D. Thyroid function test: part of the routine organic workup of new depression, but here the clear clue is substance use with slurred speech, so the drug screen comes first.
key_concept:
Psychiatric presentation with a substance clue: screen for the substance before labelling a primary disorder.
  • Slurred speech, unkempt, reported drug use: urine drug screen
  • New depression without clues: TFT, CBC, basic labs to exclude organic causes
  • Positive screen: consider substance induced mood disorder
exam_pearl: When the stem names a substance and shows an intoxication sign (slurred speech), the urine drug screen beats the routine organic labs.

stem: 2 years old has Aortic stenosis his parents brought him due to new progressive SOB during moderate exercise, ECHO: Moderate AS Most appropriate management?
why_right: The child has known aortic stenosis and now has "new progressive SOB during moderate exercise", i.e. the stenosis has become symptomatic. In valve disease the rule is that symptoms mandate intervention, and in children with congenital valvar AS the first-line intervention is percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty, which delays the need for surgical valve replacement in a growing child.
why_wrong_block:
B. Medications cannot relieve a fixed valvular obstruction or change prognosis in AS; they are only supportive (e.g., heart failure treatment while awaiting intervention). A child with new exertional symptoms needs the obstruction relieved.
C. Reassurance with echo follow-up is appropriate only for mild or asymptomatic AS; new progressive exertional dyspnoea is a warning sign (risk of syncope and sudden death) and needs intervention.
key_concept:
Valvular disease: asymptomatic = follow up; symptomatic = intervene.
  • Child with congenital valvar AS needing intervention: balloon valvuloplasty first
  • Adult symptomatic severe AS: surgical or transcatheter valve replacement
  • Red-flag symptoms in AS: exertional dyspnoea, syncope, chest pain
  • Medication does not relieve fixed obstruction
exam_pearl: In AS the symptom drives the decision more than the echo grade; in a child the intervention is balloon valvuloplasty, in an adult it is valve replacement.

stem: Down syndrome delivered 2 days ago, what is the recommended screening for this patient:
OptA: Serial abdominal x ray for another atresia "not duodenal"
why_right: Down syndrome is associated with Hirschsprung disease (as well as duodenal atresia, which would already be obvious with bilious vomiting and a double bubble). In a well 2-day-old after an uncomplicated delivery, the practical screen is to watch for passage of meconium in the first 24 to 48 hours; delay should prompt evaluation for Hirschsprung.
why_wrong_block:
A. Serial abdominal x-rays are not a screening tool; imaging is done only if there are signs of obstruction (bilious vomiting, distension). Duodenal atresia presents within hours with a double bubble rather than being found on routine films.
B. Pyloric stenosis presents at around 2 to 8 weeks with projectile non-bilious vomiting and is not a recognised Down syndrome screen; ultrasound is done only when symptoms suggest it.
D. The option says "necrotizing fasciitis" but means necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). Fecal calprotectin is not a newborn screen (levels are physiologically high in neonates), and NEC is a clinical and radiological diagnosis (feeding intolerance, bloody stool, pneumatosis), mainly in preterm infants.
key_concept:
Down syndrome GI associations: duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease.
  • Duodenal atresia: bilious vomiting in first day, double bubble
  • Hirschsprung: delayed meconium >24 to 48 h, distension
  • Also screen: echocardiogram (AVSD), congenital hypothyroidism (TSH), hearing and eyes
  • Pyloric stenosis: 2 to 8 weeks, projectile non-bilious vomiting
exam_pearl: Down syndrome + newborn who has not passed meconium by 48 hours = think Hirschsprung.

stem: Child fell down then had tonic-clonic seizure, came to the ER, drowsy but arousable, neurological exam is normal (includes pupils ... ete), best step:
OptC: Observe in the ER for 2 hours
highlight_terms_source: fell down then had tonic-clonic seizure
why_right: The child had head trauma ("fell down") followed by a tonic-clonic seizure and is still "drowsy but arousable". A post-traumatic seizure and altered level of consciousness are high-risk features for intracranial injury, so the best step is an urgent non-contrast CT head, the imaging of choice for acute bleeding, even though the neurological exam is otherwise normal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Admission for observation is the plan after CT is negative or for low-to-intermediate risk head injury; it must not replace imaging when there is a seizure and drowsiness.
C. A short ER observation period suits minor head trauma with an isolated low-risk feature and normal mental status; it is unsafe when the child has seized and remains drowsy.
D. Discharge with head-injury instructions is only for low-risk minor head trauma with normal mental status and no seizure, vomiting or loss of consciousness.
key_concept:
Paediatric head injury: high-risk features = CT now.
  • High risk: seizure, altered mental status or GCS <15, focal deficit, signs of skull fracture
  • Intermediate risk: brief LOC, vomiting, severe mechanism, severe headache: observe or CT
  • Low risk: normal mental status, no red flags: discharge with instructions
  • Acute bleed imaging: non-contrast CT
exam_pearl: A normal neurological exam does not cancel the CT when the child seized after the fall and is still drowsy.

stem: A 5-year-old girl presents with fever and burning urination. Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic?
why_right: A 5-year-old who can take oral medication with fever and dysuria has a UTI that can be managed as an outpatient. Oral antibiotics are as effective as parenteral therapy in a child who is not toxic or vomiting, so the key here is an oral agent, amoxicillin, rather than an injectable or a fluoroquinolone.
why_wrong_block:
B. IM ceftriaxone is a parenteral option for children who look toxic, are vomiting, cannot take oral medication, or are young infants; it is not needed for a well child with fever and dysuria.
C. IV ciprofloxacin is not first line in children (musculoskeletal adverse effects, resistance concerns) and is reserved for resistant or complicated infections; the IV route is also unnecessary here.
key_concept:
Paediatric UTI: route depends on how ill the child is, not the fever alone.
  • Well, tolerating oral: oral antibiotic per local E. coli susceptibility
  • Toxic, vomiting, dehydrated or young infant: parenteral (e.g., ceftriaxone)
  • Fluoroquinolones: avoid as first line in children
  • Always send urine culture before starting
exam_pearl: Fever alone does not mandate IV or IM therapy in a child who can drink and take tablets; toxicity or vomiting does.

key_concept:
Primitive reflexes: present at birth, fade in a set order.

  • ~4 months: rooting, sucking, Galant
  • ~6 months: Moro, palmar grasp
  • 12 to 18 months: Babinski
  • Parachute: appears 8 to 10 months, never disappears
exam_pearl: Stepping is the earliest reflex to go (about 2 months); a persistent primitive reflex beyond its age suggests a CNS problem such as cerebral palsy.

stem: Long term management of X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency?
key_concept:
SCID = T-cell (and B-cell) failure; only stem cell transplant cures it.
  • X-linked SCID: IL-2 receptor common gamma chain defect, boys, severe infections and failure to thrive in infancy
  • Definitive: haematopoietic stem cell transplant
  • Bridging: IVIG, PJP prophylaxis, only irradiated CMV-negative blood products, no live vaccines
  • Bruton XLA (B-cell only): lifelong IVIG is the long-term treatment
exam_pearl: Monthly immunoglobulin is the long-term answer for Bruton agammaglobulinaemia, but for SCID it is only a bridge to bone marrow transplant.

stem: An 11-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother. She is concerned of bed-wetting overnight despite toilet training and several sessions of discussion. He feels a shamed and asked help from his family and physician. Which of the following is the best management?
why_right: An 11-year-old with ongoing nocturnal enuresis who is ashamed and asking for help is keyed to a comprehensive, family centred behavioural approach. In this recall's teaching ladder, behavioural therapy (family support, no blame, reward systems, voiding before bed, evening fluid habits) is first line, the enuresis alarm second, and desmopressin third. Family involvement also addresses the child's shame and keeps him motivated.
why_wrong_block:
A. Avoiding punishment is one element of the behavioural approach, not a complete management plan on its own; the family centred package includes it.
B. Desmopressin comes after behavioural measures and the alarm in this ladder, and the intranasal form is no longer used for enuresis because of hyponatraemia and seizure risk (oral tablets or melts are used). It fits when rapid short term dryness is needed, such as a sleepover or camp.
C. The bed alarm with positive reinforcement is the second step in this ladder, used when behavioural measures fail in a motivated child and family.
key_concept:
Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis: reassure, then treat in steps.
  • Step 1: urinalysis in every child; classify primary vs secondary
  • Secondary: look for a stressor or new organic cause
  • First line: behavioural, family centred (no punishment, rewards, toileting, fluids)
  • Second line: enuresis alarm (needs motivated child and family)
  • Third line: oral desmopressin (fast effect, high relapse on stopping)
exam_pearl: Intranasal desmopressin is out for enuresis (hyponatraemia); if a drug option says 'intranasal', it is the trap.

stem: 10-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department with polyuria, polydipsia, abdominal pain, and vomiting. He is diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and is started on IV fluids and IV insulin infusion. After 2 hours of treatment, the child becomes confused and drowsy, with a decreased level of consciousness. Vital signs are stable, and blood glucose is declining steadily. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A child with DKA who becomes confused and drowsy a few hours into fluids and insulin while glucose is declining has cerebral oedema until proven otherwise, the most feared complication of paediatric DKA treatment. It is treated immediately on clinical grounds with IV mannitol (hypertonic saline is the alternative), head elevation and reduced fluid rate, before any imaging.
why_wrong_block:
B. More fluid is harmful here; overly rapid fluid replacement is linked to cerebral oedema, so the fluid rate should be reduced. Extra fluid fits shock or persistent hypovolaemia, not a falling conscious level with stable vitals.
C. Stopping insulin would let ketoacidosis rebound and does not treat raised intracranial pressure; insulin is continued, with dextrose added as glucose falls.
D. Dextrose is added to fluids when glucose falls to allow insulin to continue, but switching to dextrose fluids only does nothing for brain swelling. It would fit hypoglycaemia, which is excluded by the steadily declining but not low glucose.
key_concept:
Neurological deterioration during DKA treatment = cerebral oedema; treat at once.
  • Warning signs: headache, confusion, drowsiness, falling GCS, bradycardia with hypertension, vomiting
  • Give IV mannitol or hypertonic saline
  • Elevate head, reduce IV fluid rate
  • Check glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia
  • Imaging only after treatment has started
exam_pearl: Confusion after starting DKA treatment in a child: mannitol first, CT later; do not give more fluid.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original recall: 'Pediatric patients with DKA after corrections he becomes drowsy. How to manage? IV mannitol / IV NS bolus every 15 min. Answer: A' (IV mannitol). Better recall given as the stem.

stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with a barky cough, appears cyanotic, and has spells of breath-holding. On auscultation, you hear a monophasic wheeze. There is no inspiratory stridor noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A barky (brassy) cough, a monophasic expiratory wheeze, cyanotic spells and no inspiratory stridor point to an intrathoracic airway collapse: tracheomalacia. The floppy trachea collapses during expiration and coughing, giving a single pitch central wheeze and occasional cyanotic 'dying spells'. Diagnosis is by bronchoscopy, and it usually improves with growth.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bronchiolitis (infant under about 2 years, viral prodrome, crackles and diffuse polyphonic wheeze) and bronchitis are acute infections, not a recurrent barky cough with a fixed monophasic wheeze.
C. Laryngomalacia is supraglottic, so it causes inspiratory stridor in early infancy that worsens supine and improves prone; the stem explicitly says no inspiratory stridor.
D. Asthma gives a polyphonic, diffuse expiratory wheeze that responds to bronchodilators, not a monophasic central wheeze with a brassy barky cough.
key_concept:
Site of the airway lesion decides the noise.
  • Extrathoracic (larynx): inspiratory stridor, e.g. laryngomalacia, croup
  • Intrathoracic large airway (trachea): monophasic expiratory wheeze, barky cough, e.g. tracheomalacia
  • Small airways: polyphonic wheeze, e.g. asthma, bronchiolitis
  • Laryngomalacia diagnosis: laryngoscopy; tracheomalacia: bronchoscopy
  • Both are usually self limiting with growth
exam_pearl: Stridor on inspiration = larynx; monophasic wheeze on expiration with barky cough = trachea.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Second version (Q:): 4 year old boy with barking cough, monophonic wheeze, cyanotic, no inspiratory stridor; options Bronchiolitis / Tracheomalacia / Laryngomalacia / B. asthma. Answer: Tracheomalacia.

stem: A 2-month-old infant is brought to Well Baby Clinic by her mother because she is crying intensely recently and is not sleeping well overnight. The mother gave history of normal feeding. No fever or vomiting. These crying episodes are 2 to 3 min per week, last for 1 to 2 hours since the age of 1 month. Which of the following is the recommended revealing measure?
why_right: A 2-month-old with paroxysms of intense crying lasting 1 to 2 hours, a few times a week since 1 month, with normal feeding and no fever or vomiting, is a healthy infant with infantile colic. Colic is self limited, so management is supportive: reassure the parents and teach soothing strategies (holding, rocking, swaddling, white noise), i.e. behavioural adaptation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Feeding is normal and there is no vomiting, bloody stool or poor growth to suggest cow's milk protein allergy; routine formula changes are not recommended for colic.
B. Colic drops such as simethicone have no proven benefit, and anticholinergic drops are unsafe in young infants.
C. Respite may ease caregiver stress, but a baby sitter is not a treatment and does not teach the soothing and coping strategies that are the mainstay.
key_concept:
Infantile colic: healthy infant, crying paroxysms, self limited within the first months.
  • Rule of 3s: crying more than 3 h/day, more than 3 days/week, more than 3 weeks
  • Normal feeding, growth and examination; no fever or vomiting
  • Treatment: reassurance plus behavioural adaptation
  • No routine formula switch or medication
  • Red flags (fever, vomiting, poor growth) mean look for another cause
exam_pearl: Crying infant with normal feeding and growth: reassure and soothe; drugs or formula changes are the trap.

stem: Child came to the clinic regarding poor nutrition, he is always eating biscuits and milk and not eating well. On examination there is mild conjunctival pallor, Hb is 6.2 mg/dl with low MCV. What is the most appropriate management for this child?
OptB: Give oral iron and advise diet modification
highlight_terms_source: Hb is 6.2 mg/dl with low MCV
why_right: A child who lives on biscuits and milk with pallor, low Hb and low MCV has nutritional iron deficiency anaemia (excess milk is low in iron and displaces iron rich food). With only mild pallor and no signs of decompensation, the anaemia is chronic and tolerated, so treatment is therapeutic oral iron plus dietary change (limit milk, add iron rich foods) and follow-up to confirm a rise in Hb.
why_wrong_block:
A. Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, heart failure or acute severe symptoms; a stable child with chronic IDA corrects well with oral iron.
C. Bone marrow aspiration is invasive and not needed for typical nutritional IDA; it fits pancytopenia, blasts or suspected leukaemia or marrow failure.
D. Folate deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia; here the MCV is low, and multivitamins contain too little iron to treat established anaemia.
key_concept:
Microcytic anaemia in a toddler or child with a milk heavy diet = IDA until proven otherwise.
  • Labs: low Hb, MCV, ferritin; high TIBC and RDW
  • Treat: oral ferrous sulfate plus diet change (limit cow's milk)
  • Failure to respond to adequate iron: check adherence, then Hb electrophoresis for thalassaemia
  • Transfuse only if haemodynamically unstable or in heart failure
exam_pearl: A low Hb number alone does not mean transfusion; a stable child with chronic IDA gets oral iron.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: B (confirmed). Original recall: child only eating bread and milk, possible PICA, Hb 7; A blood transfusion / B Give oral iron and encourage healthy food. Embedded screenshot version (biscuits and milk, Hb 6): A. Give oral iron and encourage healthy food, B. Start blood transfusion; answer A. Give oral iron and encourage healthy food.

stem: Symptoms of pertussis. Management
key_concept:
Pertussis: catarrhal URTI phase, then paroxysmal whooping cough.
  • Paroxysms may end in cyanosis or post-tussive vomiting
  • Young infants may have apnoea instead of a whoop
  • Diagnosis: nasopharyngeal PCR (culture is the gold standard)
  • Treatment and close contact prophylaxis: macrolide
  • Contacts get prophylaxis even if vaccinated
exam_pearl: Whoop plus post-tussive vomiting = pertussis = macrolide for the patient and every household contact.

stem: A 7-year-old child presents with pneumonia. What is the most common causative organism?
why_right: In a school-age child (7 years) with community acquired pneumonia, the most common bacterial cause is Streptococcus pneumoniae. Neonatal organisms (Group B Streptococcus, E. coli) do not apply at this age; Mycoplasma is the main atypical alternative in older children.
why_wrong_block:
A. E. coli causes neonatal sepsis and pneumonia and is the top cause of UTI, not of community acquired pneumonia in a 7-year-old.
C. Group B Streptococcus is the leading cause of neonatal pneumonia, sepsis and meningitis (first weeks of life), not school-age pneumonia.
D. E. coli (repeated option) is a neonatal and urinary pathogen, not the common cause of childhood community acquired pneumonia.
key_concept:
Pneumonia organism by age:
  • Neonate: Group B Streptococcus, E. coli and other Gram negatives
  • Infant and preschool: viruses most common overall; S. pneumoniae is the top bacterium
  • School-age: S. pneumoniae; Mycoplasma for atypical pneumonia
  • Lobar consolidation at any age beyond the neonatal period: think S. pneumoniae
exam_pearl: Neonate = GBS and E. coli; beyond the neonatal period, typical bacterial pneumonia = S. pneumoniae.

stem: 7-year-old child presented with shortness of breath. On examination, there was unilateral dullness. X-ray showed consolidations. What is the most likely causative organism?
why_right: Unilateral dullness and consolidation on X-ray in a 7-year-old describe typical lobar pneumonia, and the most common organism for community acquired lobar pneumonia in children is Streptococcus pneumoniae.
why_wrong_block:
A. Group B streptococcus is a neonatal pathogen (pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis in the first weeks of life), not a cause of pneumonia in a 7-year-old.
C. Pseudomonas causes pneumonia in cystic fibrosis, ventilated or hospitalised and immunocompromised patients, not in a previously well child with community acquired pneumonia.
D. Haemophilus influenzae type b became rare after Hib vaccination; non-typeable H. influenzae is more typical of otitis media, sinusitis and COPD exacerbations than lobar pneumonia in children.
key_concept:
Lobar consolidation in a previously well child = S. pneumoniae.
  • Signs: dullness, bronchial breathing, crackles over one area
  • Neonate: GBS, E. coli
  • School-age atypical: Mycoplasma (patchy, extrapulmonary features)
  • Cystic fibrosis or hospital acquired: Pseudomonas
  • Post-influenza or cavitating or empyema: consider S. aureus
exam_pearl: Pseudomonas needs a reason (CF, ventilator, immunosuppression); without one, lobar pneumonia is pneumococcal.

stem: Child due for vaccination has rhinitis, coryza and conjunctivitis?
why_right: A child due for vaccination with rhinitis, coryza and conjunctivitis has a minor illness. Mild illness, with or without low grade fever, is not a contraindication to live vaccines, so MMR is given on schedule to avoid missed opportunities; only moderate or severe acute illness justifies deferral.
why_wrong_block:
B. There is no reason to drop the rubella component; MMR is given as the full combined vaccine, and a cold has no bearing on any single component.
C. Skipping or deferring the dose is wrong for a minor illness and leaves the child unprotected. Deferral fits moderate or severe illness, or a true contraindication such as severe immunodeficiency or prior anaphylaxis to the vaccine.
key_concept:
Minor illness is not a reason to delay vaccines.
  • Give: URTI, mild diarrhoea, low grade fever, on antibiotics, recovering from illness
  • Defer: moderate or severe acute illness with or without fever
  • Live vaccine contraindications: severe immunodeficiency, pregnancy, prior anaphylaxis to the vaccine
  • Egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR
  • Missed doses: give them now, do not restart the series
exam_pearl: Runny nose and red eyes on vaccination day: vaccinate; do not confuse a cold with a contraindication.

stem: Child in outpatient with chills, fever and +ve nitrite & leukocyte, asked about what to do next?
OptB: Refer to hospital for IV antibiotic
key_concept:
Febrile UTI in a child: route of antibiotics depends on clinical status, not on fever alone.
  • Well, alert, drinking: oral antibiotics as outpatient
  • Toxic, vomiting, dehydrated, cannot take orally: admit for IV antibiotics
  • Always send urine culture before the first dose
  • Nitrite + leukocyte esterase positive = high probability of UTI
exam_pearl: Fever and chills alone do not mandate IV therapy; look for the words toxic, vomiting or not tolerating oral intake before choosing admission.

stem: Pediatric with knee pain (single joint), limited range of motion, warmth, had gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago. US shows effusion. How to manage?
OptC: Synovial aspiration for analysis and culture
why_right: An acute single warm knee with limited range of motion and an effusion on US must be treated as possible septic arthritis until joint fluid proves otherwise. The preceding gastroenteritis suggests reactive arthritis, but that is a diagnosis of exclusion, so synovial aspiration with cell count, Gram stain and culture is the key step. Joint fluid examination both confirms or excludes infection and identifies the organism.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral ibuprofen: the treatment for reactive arthritis or transient synovitis once septic arthritis has been excluded. Starting it first risks missing a septic joint.
B. Oral aspirin / analgesia: aspirin is the classic treatment for rheumatic fever arthritis and is generally avoided in children otherwise (Reye syndrome). Analgesia alone does not address a possibly infected effusion.
D. IV antibiotics: right once septic arthritis is strongly suspected, but ideally after the joint is aspirated so culture is not sterilised. Here the question asks how to manage a new effusion, and aspiration comes first.
key_concept:
Acute monoarthritis with effusion = aspirate the joint.
  • Septic: fever, hot joint, refusal to move, very high synovial WBC with neutrophils, positive Gram stain or culture
  • Reactive: follows GI or GU infection by 1 to 4 weeks, sterile fluid, treated with NSAIDs
  • Transient synovitis: hip, post viral, well child, NSAIDs
  • Aspiration before antibiotics whenever possible
exam_pearl: A history of recent gastroenteritis tempts you toward reactive arthritis and NSAIDs, but a hot effusion is aspirated first because septic arthritis cannot be excluded clinically.

stem: 7 yrs old girl with type 1 DM, recently with loss of weight, glucose 250 mg/dl. What is the best advice/approach for her?
OptA: Educate the family on how to use insulin
OptB: Give her pamphlet and for follow up
OptD: Postpone education till glucose is controlled
highlight_terms_source: 7 yrs old girl with type 1 DM
key_concept:
New or poorly controlled type 1 DM in a stable child: start insulin and educate the family.
  • DKA (hyperglycaemia + acidosis + ketosis): stabilise first with fluids and IV insulin
  • No DKA: subcutaneous insulin and structured family education
  • Teach injection technique, home glucose monitoring, sick day rules
  • Most important adverse effect to teach: hypoglycaemia
exam_pearl: Weight loss in type 1 DM signals insulin deficiency, which carbohydrate restriction cannot correct; the fork is DKA (stabilise first) versus stable (insulin with family education).

stem: 7-year-old child presents with upper abdominal pain that wakes him from sleep and subsides when eating. His mother mentions that he has a history of peptic ulcer previously. What is the most diagnostic for the suspected diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: upper abdominal pain that wakes him from sleep and subsides when eating
why_right: Epigastric pain that wakes him from sleep and is relieved by eating, in a child with a previous peptic ulcer, points to a duodenal ulcer, likely related to H. pylori. The lead in asks for the most diagnostic test, and upper endoscopy (EGD) with biopsy is the gold standard: it shows the ulcer directly and the biopsy confirms H. pylori by histology, culture or rapid urease testing.
why_wrong_block:
B. Over-the-counter antacids: symptomatic treatment, not a diagnostic test; at best it would fit a mild dyspepsia question asking for initial symptom relief.
C. Give PPI: treatment of peptic ulcer disease once diagnosed (or empirical therapy in mild dyspepsia), but it diagnoses nothing and can mask H. pylori on later testing.
D. H. pylori antibiotic prophylaxis: there is no prophylactic regimen; eradication therapy is given only after H. pylori is confirmed.
key_concept:
Peptic ulcer disease: endoscopy is diagnostic, drugs are treatment.
  • Duodenal ulcer: pain relieved by food, nocturnal waking pain
  • Gastric ulcer: pain worse after food
  • Gold standard diagnosis: EGD with biopsy
  • Non invasive H. pylori tests: urea breath test, stool antigen
  • Confirmed H. pylori: triple therapy (PPI + two antibiotics)
exam_pearl: When the lead in is "most diagnostic", choose the test (EGD with biopsy), not a treatment option such as PPI or antacids.

stem: 5 years old girl came to emergency department complaining of fever, painful micturition. What is best management?
why_right: This recall's key is oral ampicillin: a 5 year old girl with painful micturition and fever who is not described as toxic or vomiting can be managed with an oral antibiotic. A closely matching question on uncomplicated cystitis in a 5 year old girl is keyed to oral amoxicillin (an aminopenicillin like ampicillin), which supports an oral aminopenicillin here.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oral something: the recall does not name this drug. If it was an oral cephalosporin (cephalexin, cefixime) it would also be a reasonable oral choice; the source keyed ampicillin.
C. IV ciprofloxacin: fluoroquinolones are not first line in children because of cartilage toxicity concerns, and IV therapy is reserved for toxic children or those who cannot take oral medication.
D. IM ceftriaxone: used for children who are vomiting or too unwell for oral therapy, or as a single dose before oral step down; unnecessary for a child who can take oral antibiotics.
key_concept:
Childhood UTI: oral antibiotics unless the child is toxic or cannot tolerate oral intake.
  • Most common organism: E. coli
  • Well child: oral antibiotic after urine culture
  • Toxic, vomiting, dehydrated, young infant: IV or IM (e.g. ceftriaxone)
  • Avoid fluoroquinolones as first line in children
exam_pearl: In a well child, the route matters more than the drug name; reject IV and IM options unless the stem says toxic or vomiting.

stem: Child brought by his mother with lethargy, pallor, low grade subjective fever, lymphadenopathy for 2 months. What to do next?
why_right: Lethargy, pallor, low grade fever and lymphadenopathy for 2 months in a child raise concern for leukaemia. The lead in is what to do next and no labs have been done yet, so the first step is a CBC with peripheral blood film, which can show cytopenias and blasts. Bone marrow examination follows to confirm the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Virology screening: right when the picture suggests infectious mononucleosis or another viral cause (sore throat, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes on film). It does not address the malignancy red flags here and still needs a blood film first.
C. Bone marrow examination: the confirmatory test for leukaemia, done after the blood film is abnormal (blasts or cytopenias). It is not the first investigation when no blood count has been done.
key_concept:
Suspected childhood leukaemia: initial vs confirmatory test.
  • Next or initial step: CBC with peripheral blood film
  • Confirmatory: bone marrow aspiration and biopsy
  • Red flags: persistent pallor and fatigue, unexplained fever, lymphadenopathy, bruising, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly
exam_pearl: Same stem, different lead in: "next" means blood film, "confirmatory" means bone marrow examination.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot note: No labs. A) blood film, confirmed by Hatim 100/120 in pediatric. Pallor + next (CBC not done, just pallor + lymphadenopathy, no thrombocytopenia) = blood film; initial to confirm / confirmatory = bone marrow.

stem: Child brought by his mother with lethargy, pallor, low grade subjective fever, lymphadenopathy for 2 months. What is the confirmatory test?
why_right: Lethargy, pallor, low grade fever and lymphadenopathy for 2 months in a child suggests leukaemia. The lead in asks for the confirmatory test, and bone marrow examination (aspiration and biopsy) is definitively diagnostic, establishing the blast percentage and lineage.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood film: the initial or next step, showing cytopenias or circulating blasts, but it cannot confirm leukaemia or classify it. It is the answer when the lead in asks what to do next.
B. Virology screening: right when a viral illness such as infectious mononucleosis is suspected; it does not confirm or exclude leukaemia.
key_concept:
Suspected childhood leukaemia: initial vs confirmatory test.
  • Initial: CBC with peripheral blood film
  • Confirmatory: bone marrow aspiration and biopsy
  • Bone marrow also allows immunophenotyping and cytogenetics
exam_pearl: "Confirmatory" in the lead in flips the answer from blood film to bone marrow examination.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Different recall from a friend exactly saying 'What is the confirmatory test?' Answer is C) bone marrow examination (confirmed).

stem: A child had chest pain, sore throat or some sort of infection, then he got pain in his right knee while left is perfect. How can you treat? There is redness and slight effusion on physical examination.
why_right: A child with a preceding sore throat who then develops a red knee with effusion (and possibly chest pain, suggesting carditis) fits post streptococcal disease, most likely acute rheumatic fever. The main symptomatic treatment of rheumatic fever arthritis and mild carditis is high dose oral acetylsalicylic acid, which gives a rapid response, so the source keys aspirin.
why_wrong_block:
B. Steroids: reserved for moderate to severe rheumatic carditis (e.g. heart failure); not the treatment for arthritis.
C. Reassurance: inappropriate because rheumatic fever needs anti-inflammatory treatment, eradication of group A strep with penicillin and secondary prophylaxis.
D. Other medication: unspecified in the recall; penicillin is also given to eradicate streptococci, but the symptomatic arthritis treatment asked for here is aspirin.
key_concept:
Acute rheumatic fever management.
  • Arthritis and mild carditis: high dose aspirin (or NSAID)
  • Moderate to severe carditis: add corticosteroids
  • Eradicate group A strep: penicillin
  • Secondary prophylaxis: long term benzathine penicillin
  • Diagnosis: Jones criteria with evidence of preceding strep infection
exam_pearl: Rheumatic arthritis is classically migratory polyarthritis with a dramatic response to aspirin; a single joint after sore throat may instead be post streptococcal reactive arthritis, which is treated with NSAIDs.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recaller: 'My recall is bad on this one.' Pretty sure there was no investigation; chose ASA thinking it might be rheumatic fever related, however might be recall bias.

stem: 6 weeks presented w jaundice and alcoholic stool and he also has pulmonary stenosis, butterfly vertebrae and triangular face What is the possible diagnosis ?
why_right: Cholestatic jaundice with acholic (pale) stools at 6 weeks combined with pulmonary stenosis, butterfly vertebrae and a triangular face is the classic picture of Alagille syndrome. It is an autosomal dominant disorder (JAG1 or NOTCH2) with paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts, and the extrahepatic features distinguish it from biliary atresia.
why_wrong_block: A. Duodenal atresia: presents in the first days of life with bilious vomiting and a double bubble on X-ray, often with Down syndrome; it does not cause cholestatic jaundice with pale stools or butterfly vertebrae.
key_concept:
Neonatal cholestasis with pale stools: think biliary atresia vs Alagille syndrome.
  • Alagille: paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts + pulmonary stenosis + butterfly vertebrae + triangular face + posterior embryotoxon
  • Biliary atresia: isolated cholestasis with pale stools, needs urgent Kasai
  • Duodenal atresia: bilious vomiting, double bubble, Down syndrome
exam_pearl: Cholestasis with pale stools alone suggests biliary atresia; add a heart murmur (pulmonary stenosis) and butterfly vertebrae and it becomes Alagille syndrome.

stem: A newborn with Hemophilia A presents with bleeding. What is the appropriate treatment?
key_concept:
Haemophilia A bleeding: replace the missing factor.
  • Haemophilia A: factor VIII deficiency, prolonged aPTT, normal PT and platelets
  • Haemophilia B: factor IX deficiency, treat with factor IX
  • Inhibitors present: recombinant factor VIIa (bypassing agent)
  • Specific factor unavailable: cryoprecipitate or FFP
exam_pearl: Factor VII vs factor VIII is a classic recall slip; rFVIIa is only for haemophilia with inhibitors.

stem: A well circumscribed red swelling under the conjunctiva
key_concept:
Red eye nodule: decide by pain, colour and blanching.
  • Episcleritis: mild or no pain, bright red, mobile, blanches with phenylephrine, self limiting
  • Scleritis: severe boring pain, violaceous, tender, non blanching, vision threatening
  • Scleritis: look for RA, vasculitis; needs urgent ophthalmology and systemic therapy
  • Flat bright red patch with no swelling: subconjunctival hemorrhage
exam_pearl: Severe pain is the single feature that moves a localised red eye from episcleritis to scleritis.

stem: A 10-year-old boy presents to the clinic complaining of abdominal pain, frequent diarrhoea that is sometimes bloody, and pain usually accompanying defecation. His mother observed that he has lost weight over the last 3 months since the onset of the problem. The boy also has aches and pains of his joints. On examination, he looks ill, pale, with a so> abdomen, no tenderness or organomegaly (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: frequent diarrhoea that is sometimes bloody
aches and pains of his joints
why_right: A child with chronic diarrhea that is "sometimes bloody", pain accompanying defecation (rectal involvement, tenesmus/urgency), weight loss over 3 months, pallor and joint aches has inflammatory bowel disease. Visible blood in the stool tips the choice to ulcerative colitis, a continuous mucosal colitis starting at the rectum. Arthralgia is a common extraintestinal manifestation of IBD, and anemia with low albumin reflects chronic inflammation and blood/protein loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Celiac disease gives non-bloody malabsorptive diarrhea, distension and poor growth; it does not explain bloody stools with painful defecation and arthralgia.
B. Crohn's disease also causes weight loss, anemia and arthralgia, but stools are usually non-bloody with periumbilical/RLQ pain, oral ulcers or perianal disease; with frank bloody diarrhea, choose UC.
D. Chronic dysentery (e.g. amoebic or persistent bacterial) can give prolonged bloody diarrhea, but stool microscopy/culture would show the organism and it does not explain arthralgia as an extraintestinal feature; this cluster in a child is IBD.
key_concept:
Chronic diarrhea + weight loss + extraintestinal signs in a child = IBD; blood decides the type.
  • UC: bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, rectum upward, continuous
  • Crohn's: non-bloody, RLQ pain/mass, oral ulcers, perianal fistula, skip lesions
  • Extraintestinal: arthritis/arthralgia, erythema nodosum, uveitis, growth failure
  • Labs: anemia, low albumin, raised CRP/ESR
  • Confirm: ileocolonoscopy with biopsy
exam_pearl: Bloody diarrhea with IBD features: pick UC over Crohn's; if UC is not listed, Crohn's becomes the answer.

stem: 12 years old presented with fever and night sweat and painless cervical lymph nodes enlargment FNA: show Reed–Sternberg cells What the diagnosis?
why_right: Reed–Sternberg cells on cytology are the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma. The picture fits: an older child/adolescent with painless cervical lymphadenopathy plus B symptoms (fever, night sweats). Note that FNA is suggestive only; definitive diagnosis and subtyping require excisional lymph node biopsy.
why_wrong_block: A. AML presents with marrow failure (pallor, bleeding, infections), blasts on the blood film and sometimes gum infiltration; it does not show Reed–Sternberg cells in a lymph node.
key_concept:
Painless cervical nodes + B symptoms in a teen = think lymphoma; Reed–Sternberg cell = Hodgkin.
  • B symptoms: fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss
  • Hodgkin: contiguous nodal spread, often mediastinal mass, bimodal age
  • Non-Hodgkin (e.g. Burkitt, lymphoblastic): rapid growth, extranodal, abdominal or mediastinal mass
  • Diagnosis: excisional node biopsy (FNA is not enough)
  • Alternatives to exclude: reactive nodes, TB lymphadenitis
exam_pearl: Reed–Sternberg (owl's eye) cell = Hodgkin; a node that is painful with alcohol is a classic Hodgkin clue.

stem: 3 day age neonate c/s delivery have desaturation and grunting also blue lips around mouth
key_concept:
Newborn respiratory distress: decide by gestation, onset and CXR.
  • TTN: term CS, onset within hours, fissural fluid, settles by 2 to 3 days
  • RDS: preterm, onset at birth, ground glass + air bronchograms, low volumes
  • Pneumonia/sepsis: risk factors, any time, patchy infiltrates
  • Meconium aspiration: post term, stained liquor, hyperinflation with patchy opacities
exam_pearl: CS + term + early onset = TTN; if the baby is preterm think RDS, if distress appears or persists beyond the first days think infection.

stem: 3 (weeks old or days old baby) presented to the ER with lethargy poor feeding, hypotonia, irritability (i think), his bedside glucose was 35 mg/dl. Critical labs was drown before glucose correction. Lab results: beta-hydroxybutyrate levels 0.1 (Normal >1.5) Glucose 2.2 mmol/l (low) Fasting insulin 44 (i think normal) Cortisol 4 hours above normal (i think slightly high) Other labs normal
why_right: The critical sample shows hypoglycemia with low beta-hydroxybutyrate (0.1), meaning hypoketotic hypoglycemia, together with an insulin level that is detectable/high while glucose is low. Insulin should be suppressed during hypoglycemia, so inappropriate insulin plus suppressed ketones (insulin blocks lipolysis and ketogenesis) defines hyperinsulinism. In a neonate with lethargy, poor feeding and hypotonia this is congenital hyperinsulinism.
why_wrong_block:
A. Adrenal insufficiency causes ketotic hypoglycemia with low cortisol (often hyponatremia and hyperkalemia); here cortisol is not low and ketones are suppressed.
B. Glycogen storage disease type I gives fasting hypoglycemia with hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis and hyperlipidemia, with insulin appropriately suppressed.
D. Growth hormone deficiency (often as hypopituitarism with cortisol deficiency) causes hypoglycemia with appropriately suppressed insulin; neonatal clues are microphallus, midline defects and prolonged jaundice, none given here.
key_concept:
Read the critical sample: ketones + insulin sort neonatal hypoglycemia.
  • Low ketones + inappropriately high insulin: hyperinsulinism
  • Low ketones + low insulin: fatty acid oxidation defect
  • Suppressed insulin + low cortisol/GH: adrenal or pituitary deficiency
  • Hepatomegaly + lactic acidosis: glycogen storage disease I
  • Hyperinsulinism also: high glucose need, glucagon response
exam_pearl: Any measurable insulin during hypoglycemia is inappropriate; hypoketotic + insulin present = hyperinsulinism.

stem: Female patient came 2 weeks after delivery with mood swings and feeling overwhelmed, she has no thought to harm herself or her baby. She is breastfeeding. She has good social support. What to do?
OptD: encourage her (or support her) and follow up her
highlight_terms_source: no thought to harm herself or her baby
why_right: Mood swings and feeling overwhelmed in the first 2 weeks after delivery, with "no thought to harm herself or her baby" and "good social support", fit postpartum (baby) blues. Blues is self limiting and usually settles within about 2 weeks, so treatment is support and advice, with follow up to make sure symptoms resolve and do not evolve into postpartum depression. This is why "support her and follow up" is better than reassurance alone.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stop breastfeeding: never needed for blues, and even in postpartum depression many antidepressants are compatible with breastfeeding.
B. Reassure: correct in spirit, but reassurance alone omits follow up. At 2 weeks, persisting symptoms would point to postpartum depression, so she must be reviewed.
C. Antidepressants: right for postpartum depression (symptoms beyond 2 weeks, anhedonia, guilt, functional impairment), not for short lived blues.
key_concept:
Postpartum mood disorders are separated mainly by timing, duration and severity.
  • Baby blues: starts in the first days, lasts up to about 2 weeks, mild, function preserved: support, education, follow up
  • Postpartum depression: persists beyond 2 weeks, anhedonia, guilt, impaired function: psychotherapy with or without SSRI
  • Postpartum psychosis: hallucinations, delusions, confusion: emergency admission
exam_pearl: Duration is the discriminator: symptoms still present past 2 weeks are no longer blues, so blues always needs follow up.

stem: A 12 years old female (I think) had a loss of consciousness after sitting in the sun for sometime. what is the red flag for this patient?
OptD: Family history of early unexplained death
highlight_terms_source: loss of consciousness after sitting in the sun
why_right: Syncope after sitting in the sun (heat, prolonged posture) is usually vasovagal (reflex) syncope and benign. The red flag that suggests a cardiac cause is a family history of early unexplained (sudden) death, which raises inherited arrhythmia syndromes (long QT, Brugada) or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and mandates ECG and cardiac evaluation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Brief jerky movements commonly occur during vasovagal syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion (convulsive syncope) and are not by themselves a red flag.
B. Dizziness, lightheadedness or blurred vision before LOC is a typical vasovagal prodrome and is reassuring.
C. Option not recalled; judge any remaining choice against the cardiac red flag list below.
key_concept:
Syncope red flags point to a cardiac cause.
  • Family history of sudden or unexplained death at a young age
  • Syncope during exertion or while supine
  • Preceded by palpitations or chest pain, no prodrome
  • Triggered by loud noise, fright or swimming (long QT)
  • Abnormal ECG or murmur
  • Benign: prodrome, prolonged standing, heat, quick recovery
exam_pearl: Prodrome and heat point to vasovagal; family sudden death, exertion or no warning means ECG and cardiology.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option C not recalled (printed as a stray 'C' after option B).

stem: 7 month child with asthma symptoms what is the diagnostic test
key_concept:
Under 5 years asthma is diagnosed clinically.
  • Recurrent wheeze/cough, triggers, atopy or family history
  • Response to bronchodilator or controller trial
  • Infant wheeze: consider bronchiolitis, foreign body, reflux, CF, malformations
  • Spirometry from about 5 to 6 years
exam_pearl: If the answer list has 'history, exam and response to bronchodilator', that wins in a young child; spirometry only for school age.

stem: A boy presented with polyuria, polydipsia, and nocturia Urine osmolality 120 Serum osmolality 300 (Numbers are not accurate) Water deprivation test: After giving desmopressin urine osmolality improved. What is the best long-term management?
highlight_terms_source: After giving desmopressin urine osmolality improved
why_right: Polyuria and polydipsia with dilute urine (low urine osmolality) and high serum osmolality is diabetes insipidus. The urine fails to concentrate with water deprivation but concentrates after desmopressin, proving the kidney responds to ADH, so the defect is ADH deficiency (central DI). Long-term treatment is replacement with desmopressin.
why_wrong_block: A. Fluid restriction is dangerous in DI (worsens dehydration and hypernatremia); it is the treatment of SIADH, and water restriction is only used diagnostically under supervision.
key_concept:
Water deprivation then desmopressin separates the polyurias.
  • Concentrates with deprivation: primary polydipsia
  • No rise with deprivation, rises with desmopressin: central DI, treat with desmopressin
  • No rise with either: nephrogenic DI, treat with thiazide + low salt diet (stop the offending drug)
  • Causes of central DI: head trauma, surgery, craniopharyngioma, LCH
exam_pearl: Response to desmopressin = central DI; no response = nephrogenic DI, where thiazides are used.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed version: pediatric with polydipsia, polyuria, urine osmolality 150, serum osmolality 350; no change after fluid deprivation but osmolality increased with vasopressin; long-term medication? Options: Desmopressin (DDAVP) [highlighted]; i forgot but i think steroids?

stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with chronic diarrhea, blood in stool, weight loss, and fever. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: chronic diarrhea, blood in stool, weight loss, and fever
key_concept:
Chronic bloody diarrhea + weight loss + fever in a child = suspect IBD.
  • Exclude infection: stool cultures, C. difficile
  • Bloods: CBC, CRP/ESR, albumin; fecal calprotectin
  • Diagnostic: ileocolonoscopy with biopsies (+ upper endoscopy in children)
  • Severe or toxic: admit, IV fluids, IV steroids
exam_pearl: Red flags (blood, weight loss, fever) mean investigate, not treat symptomatically; acid suppression is never the answer for bloody diarrhea.

stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with chronic diarrhea, blood in stool, weight loss, and fever. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: chronic diarrhea, blood in stool, weight loss, and fever

Suspected pediatric IBD: stable = endoscopy with biopsy; toxic = admit.

  • CBC, CRP/ESR, albumin, fecal calprotectin
  • Ileocolonoscopy + upper endoscopy with biopsies confirm
  • MR enterography for small bowel extent
