stem: 4-year-old child is brought to the clinic for a check-up. When performing a cover test, the child's deft eye moves laterally when the right eye is covered. The family hesitate to start treatment Which of the following is the most serious complication?
highlight_terms_source: moves laterally when the right eye is covered
why_right: On the cover test, the uncovered left eye moving to take up fixation when the right is covered means the left eye was deviated at rest: a manifest squint in a 4-year-old. Because the family "hesitate to start treatment", the brain keeps suppressing the image from the deviated eye, and this leads to amblyopia, a permanent loss of vision if not treated within the visual development window. That irreversible vision loss is why amblyopia is the most serious complication.
why_wrong_block:
A. Strabismus is the condition already present (the cover test shows it), not its complication.
B. Nystagmus is a separate oscillation disorder (congenital, or from early severe visual loss or neurological disease); it is not the expected result of untreated squint.
D. Leukocoria is a white pupillary reflex from retinoblastoma or cataract; it can be a CAUSE of squint, not a consequence of untreated squint.
key_concept:
Untreated childhood squint → suppression of the deviated eye → amblyopia (lazy eye).
  • Cover test: the uncovered eye moving to fixate = manifest squint (tropia)
  • Eye moves outward to fixate = it was turned in (esotropia); moves inward = exotropia
  • Screening at any age: corneal light reflex (Hirschberg) and red reflex
  • Treatment: correct refractive error (glasses), patching or atropine penalization of the good eye, surgery for alignment
  • Results are best when treated early in childhood
exam_pearl: Any squint in a child needs ophthalmology review; leukocoria with squint means exclude retinoblastoma first.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot 'Q:' version: 5 years old girl with convergent squint for the last two years, mother hesitated to start treatment; complication? Cataract / amblyopia ✅ / Optic neuritis / Retinal detachment.

stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the Primary Clinic because her mother noticed she is pale. She has a history of drinking cow’s milk and biscuit daily and didn’t eat red meat low hbg low mcv low ferritin A slight increase in reticulocyte count around 1.8 and normal was 1.2 What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: low hbg low mcv low ferritin
key_concept:
Low ferritin is the decisive test for iron deficiency.
  • Toddler + excess cow's milk + no meat = iron deficiency
  • Cow's milk: iron poor, displaces solids, occult GI loss
  • Thal trait: microcytosis, normal ferritin, high RBC count
  • Chronic disease: ferritin normal/high
  • Spherocytosis: hemolysis, high retics, spherocytes
exam_pearl: Ferritin decides: low ferritin = iron deficiency; normal or high ferritin with microcytosis points to thalassemia trait or chronic disease.

stem: Pedia (7 months maybe) Constant squint/converge
why_right: Intermittent misalignment can be normal in the first few months of life, but a CONSTANT squint ("constant ... converge") at about 7 months is never physiological. It needs referral to ophthalmology to exclude an organic cause (refractive error, cataract, retinoblastoma) and to prevent amblyopia.
why_wrong_block: A. Observation is only acceptable for intermittent deviation in early infancy (roughly the first 4 months); waiting until 24 months with a constant squint risks amblyopia and a missed tumour or cataract.
key_concept:
Squint in infants: intermittent and early = can observe; constant or persisting = refer.
  • Constant squint at any age → ophthalmology referral
  • Any squint persisting beyond early infancy → referral
  • Always check the red reflex: leukocoria with squint suggests retinoblastoma or cataract
  • Untreated squint → amblyopia
exam_pearl: The word "constant" flips the answer from observe to refer, whatever the age.

stem: 6 months old infant brought to vaccination clinic He had huge swelling at injection site when previous DTaP given Now he have URTI with temperature 37.9 What to do regarding Dtap vaccine ?
highlight_terms_source: huge swelling at injection site when previous DTaP
why_right: Give the DTaP dose now. A "huge swelling at injection site" after the previous dose is a local reaction, which is not a contraindication to further DTaP doses, and a mild URTI with a temperature of 37.9 is a minor illness that should not delay vaccination. Deferring for trivial reasons only leaves the infant unprotected against pertussis at the age it is most dangerous.
why_wrong_block:
B. There is no required waiting interval after a local reaction; delaying 2 months leaves the infant unprotected and off schedule for no benefit.
C. Only a moderate or severe acute illness justifies postponing a vaccine; a mild URTI with low grade temperature does not, so waiting for it to resolve is a missed opportunity.
D. Dropping the pertussis component (DT) is reserved for true pertussis contraindications such as encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose; a local swelling is not one of them.
key_concept:
Local reactions and minor illness are NOT reasons to withhold or delay DTaP.
  • Redness, swelling (even large), low or moderate fever after a dose: reassure and continue schedule
  • Mild illness (URTI, low grade fever): vaccinate now
  • Moderate or severe acute illness: postpone until improved
  • Encephalopathy within 7 days of a pertussis dose: contraindication, give DT
  • Progressive or unstable neurological disorder: withhold until stabilized
  • Anaphylaxis to a previous dose or component: contraindication
exam_pearl: Large local swelling plus a sniffle is still a 'vaccinate today' case; only encephalopathy or anaphylaxis changes the DTaP plan.

stem: 6 or 4 years old child with DM type 1 complaining of repeated hypoglycemia at night, his current medication's are rapid acting insulin before meal and basal insulin at night what is the most appropriate modification on his current regimen:
OptB: decrease the dose of basal insulin
why_right: The hypoglycemia is "at night" and the only insulin acting overnight is the "basal insulin at night", so the basal dose is too high and should be reduced. Matching the adjustment to the timing of the low is the rule: fasting or nocturnal lows point to basal insulin, lows after meals point to prandial insulin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Waking a young child for a 3 AM meal treats the symptom, not the cause, and is impractical; the fix is to lower the excess basal insulin.
C. Rapid acting insulin before meals causes lows in the hours after meals; it would be reduced if the hypoglycemia were postprandial, not nocturnal.
D. Feeding extra carbohydrate to cover too much insulin leads to weight gain and erratic control; it does not correct the overdosed basal insulin.
key_concept:
Adjust the insulin that is acting when the low occurs.
  • Nocturnal or fasting hypoglycemia: reduce basal (long acting) insulin
  • Postprandial hypoglycemia: reduce the prandial (rapid acting) dose before that meal
  • Both: reduce both
  • Exercise related lows: reduce the pre exercise prandial dose
  • Never stop basal insulin in type 1 DM (risk of DKA)
  • New recurrent lows soon after diagnosis: think honeymoon period
exam_pearl: Timing decides the insulin: night lows = basal, after meal lows = bolus.

stem: child presented with short stature, mild jaundice and he is pale with frontal bossing and maxillary and hepatosplenomegaly and lossing weight What is the important investigating to short stature ?
highlight_terms_source: pale with frontal bossing and maxillary
why_right: The clues pale, mild jaundice, frontal bossing, maxillary prominence and hepatosplenomegaly describe chronic hemolytic anemia with extramedullary erythropoiesis, classically beta thalassemia major. Here the short stature and weight loss are secondary to the anemia, so the key first investigation is the hemoglobin (CBC), followed by indices and hemoglobin electrophoresis to confirm the type.
why_wrong_block:
A. The jaundice here is hemolytic (unconjugated) and the organomegaly is from extramedullary hematopoiesis, so LFTs do not identify the cause; they matter later for iron overload liver damage.
C. TSH is part of the work up of unexplained short stature (hypothyroid child: short, overweight, delayed bone age), but this child has a clear hemolytic picture that explains the growth failure.
D. Pituitary (growth hormone) testing fits a short child with low IGF-1, delayed bone age and otherwise normal exam, not one with pallor, jaundice and skeletal marrow expansion.
key_concept:
Short stature with pallor, jaundice, frontal bossing and hepatosplenomegaly = chronic hemolytic anemia (beta thalassemia major).
  • First test: hemoglobin / CBC (severe microcytic anemia)
  • Then reticulocytes, blood film and hemoglobin electrophoresis (raised HbF and HbA2)
  • Frontal bossing, maxillary overgrowth (chipmunk face): marrow expansion
  • Hepatosplenomegaly: extramedullary erythropoiesis
  • Endocrine causes (TSH, GH) are tested when there is no systemic clue
exam_pearl: When a short child has a systemic disease picture, test the disease (Hb here), not the growth hormones.

stem: 10 years old come to your clinic with dental caries, high consumption of chocolate and sugar, and low vegetables and fruit intake, what is the prevention point of counselling?
highlight_terms_source: high consumption of chocolate and sugar
why_right: The child's caries are driven by his diet: "high consumption of chocolate and sugar" with "low vegetables and fruit". The prevention point is therefore dietary counselling: cutting the amount and especially the frequency of sugary snacks and drinks and building a balanced diet, which addresses the cause rather than one adjunct.
why_wrong_block:
B. Caries is caused by free sugars and how often they are eaten, not carbohydrate in general; a blanket 'eat less carb' message is too narrow and misses the fruit and vegetable deficit.
C. Fluoride is a useful adjunct to strengthen enamel, but it does not remove the cause; the main counselling point when diet is clearly the problem is dietary change.
key_concept:
Caries prevention in children starts with the cause.
  • Diet: reduce frequency and amount of free sugars, sweets and sugary drinks
  • Oral hygiene: twice daily brushing with fluoride toothpaste
  • Fluoride supplements, varnish or mouthwash: adjuncts per dentist and age
  • Toddlers: no bottle in bed (nursing bottle caries)
  • Regular dental visits
exam_pearl: When the stem spells out a bad diet, the counselling answer is diet, not a fluoride product.

stem: A 34-week preterm infant was delivered using vacuum extraction (ventouse). On day 2 of life, the baby appears pale and lethargic. On physical examination, there is a fluctuant scalp swelling that crosses suture lines and is increasing in size. Laboratory investigations show: Hemoglobin: Low, Platelets: Normal, PT: Normal, PTT: Normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: fluctuant scalp swelling that crosses suture lines
why_right: After a vacuum (ventouse) delivery, a fluctuant scalp swelling that crosses suture lines and is increasing in size with a baby who is pale and lethargic and has low hemoglobin is a subgaleal hemorrhage. The subgaleal space can hold a large part of a neonate's blood volume, so this is hypovolemic shock: the next step is resuscitation with volume and packed RBC transfusion. Normal platelets, PT and PTT mean the bleed is mechanical, not a coagulopathy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation fits caput succedaneum (soft, crosses sutures, maximal at birth and shrinking) or cephalohematoma (limited by sutures, stable baby); a growing swelling with pallor, lethargy and low Hb is life threatening.
B. IV antibiotics would be for sepsis or an infected cephalohematoma (fever, erythema); here the picture is acute blood loss, not infection.
C. The option text was not recalled; whatever it was (e.g. vitamin K or plasma), it cannot outrank volume and blood replacement in a shocked, anemic baby with normal coagulation.
key_concept:
Neonatal scalp swellings after delivery:
  • Caput succedaneum: soft edema, crosses sutures, largest at birth, resolves in days: reassure
  • Cephalohematoma: subperiosteal, does NOT cross sutures, firm edge, may cause jaundice: observe
  • Subgaleal hemorrhage: fluctuant, crosses sutures, expands after birth, pallor, tachycardia, shock, falling Hb: emergency
  • Subgaleal: classic after vacuum extraction
  • Management: volume and packed RBCs, monitor head circumference and Hb, correct any coagulopathy
exam_pearl: Crosses sutures plus enlarging plus pale baby = subgaleal hemorrhage, not caput; transfuse, do not observe.

stem: 7y present to the ER c/o 5 day hx of SOB with white sputum which get yellow after a while, was dx with pneumonia which was treated with ABx and get better. 2 days after, start to have SOB and his symptoms get worse, 85% on RA. Vitals BP 90/70 HR 123 Temp 37. VBG PCO2 70 PO2 45 pH 7.2 (or 7.1, the unit was not the usual unit of pH). What is the most likely cause of his presentation?
why_right: The gas shows PCO2 70 with pH 7.2 (acute respiratory acidosis) and the child is hypoxic at 85% on room air, tachycardic (HR 123) with a narrow pulse pressure. Failure of both oxygenation and ventilation after worsening pneumonia is acute respiratory failure (hypercapnic, type 2, with hypoxemia), which is the diagnosis that explains the whole picture and dictates urgent ventilatory support.
why_wrong_block:
A. 'Complication of pneumonia' is too vague to be the answer; the gas pins down the specific complication, which is failure of gas exchange.
B. ARDS needs bilateral opacities on imaging and a low PaO2/FiO2 ratio with PEEP, and early ARDS usually gives hypoxemia with low or normal CO2; neither imaging nor these criteria are provided here, while the marked CO2 retention fits respiratory failure.
D. A parapneumonic effusion would be suggested by dullness, reduced breath sounds and a fluid level on X-ray; it does not by itself explain a PCO2 of 70 with acidosis.
key_concept:
Read the gas to classify respiratory failure.
  • Type 1 (hypoxemic): low PaO2, normal or low PaCO2 (pneumonia, aspiration, early ARDS)
  • Type 2 (hypercapnic): high PaCO2 with acidosis (fatigue, airway or neuromuscular failure)
  • Acute type 2: pH falls with rising CO2
  • On a VBG, judge oxygenation by SpO2, not venous PO2
  • ARDS: Berlin criteria (timing within 1 week, bilateral opacities, PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 on PEEP, not cardiac)
exam_pearl: High CO2 with acidosis in a tiring child = respiratory failure; ARDS needs bilateral infiltrates you were not shown.

stem: 28 weeks neonate developed desaturation and bradycardia improving with stimulation. What's the underlying cause?
highlight_terms_source: desaturation and bradycardia improving with stimulation
why_right: A 28 week neonate with episodes of desaturation and bradycardia that improve with stimulation has apnea of prematurity. Its cause is the immature brainstem (central) control of breathing, which is why it is inversely related to gestational age, responds to tactile stimulation and is treated with caffeine.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypoglycemia can trigger apnea and must be excluded, but it is a secondary cause shown by a low glucose; the stem gives a typical premature infant with no metabolic clue.
B. Meconium aspiration affects term or post term babies born through meconium stained liquor and causes persistent respiratory distress, not intermittent self limiting spells in a 28 week infant.
C. Airway malformations give obstructive symptoms (stridor, distress, feeding difficulty) that do not resolve with simple stimulation.
key_concept:
Apnea of prematurity: central immaturity of respiratory control.
  • Pause of 20 seconds or more, or shorter with bradycardia or desaturation
  • More frequent the more premature the baby
  • Responds to stimulation
  • Exclude secondary causes: sepsis, hypoglycemia, anemia, IVH, temperature instability
  • Treatment: stimulation, caffeine, CPAP if persistent
  • Resolves as the infant matures
exam_pearl: Preterm spells that stop with a flick of the foot = apnea of prematurity (central), treat with caffeine.

stem: Pediatric (not sure about the age) patient with clear case of brucellosis. Hx of drink raw milk from goat, patient had pain in the knee. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
key_concept:
Brucellosis treatment is combination therapy for weeks.
  • Age 8 years or older and adults: doxycycline plus rifampicin (or streptomycin) for 6 weeks
  • Younger than 8 years: TMP-SMX plus rifampicin
  • Spondylitis or sacroiliitis: extend to about 12 weeks
  • Neurobrucellosis: months of therapy
  • Pregnancy: avoid doxycycline
  • Monotherapy: high relapse
exam_pearl: In pediatric brucellosis, the child's age (8 years) decides doxycycline vs TMP-SMX.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler note: Age > 8 years: Doxycycline; Age < 8 years: TMP SMX. (Age not recalled, so no option marked.)
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 13 year old boy has arthritis and when he exercises he has joint pain and chest pain. He started to take penicillin G monthly. When will he stop taking penicillin?
why_right: A 13 year old with arthritis plus chest pain on exertion is being treated as rheumatic fever with carditis. With carditis, secondary prophylaxis continues for 10 years after the last attack or until age 21, whichever is longer: 13 + 10 = age 23, which is longer than age 21.
why_wrong_block:
A. 2 years is shorter than any recommended duration of secondary prophylaxis after rheumatic fever.
B. 5 years after the attack (age 18) is the rule only for rheumatic fever without carditis, and even then it continues until 21 if that is longer.
D. Until age 21 is the answer for rheumatic fever without carditis in this age group (5 years or to 21, whichever longer); carditis extends it to 10 years.
key_concept:
Secondary prophylaxis: whichever is LONGER of years since last attack or the age limit.
  • No carditis: 5 years or until age 21
  • Carditis, no residual valve disease: 10 years or until age 21
  • Carditis with residual valve disease: 10 years or until age 40 (lifelong may be needed)
  • Drug: monthly IM benzathine penicillin
  • Do the arithmetic: age at attack plus years, then compare with the age limit
exam_pearl: Chest pain or carditis in the stem switches 5 years to 10 years; add it to the current age before comparing with 21.

stem: 2 y.o evaluated for squint, white pupil instead of red reflex, how to diagnose?
highlight_terms_source: white pupil instead of red reflex
why_right: A 2-year-old with squint and "white pupil instead of red reflex" (leukocoria) has retinoblastoma until proven otherwise. Among the imaging options, MRI is preferred because it defines intraocular extent and optic nerve and intracranial spread without radiation, which matters since hereditary retinoblastoma carries a high risk of radiation-induced second cancers. Clinical diagnosis itself is by dilated fundus examination under anaesthesia by an ophthalmologist.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT shows the characteristic calcification but is avoided because of radiation exposure in a child who may carry an RB1 germline mutation.
C. Ocular ultrasound is a useful bedside test showing a calcified intraocular mass, but it cannot assess optic nerve or intracranial extension; it would be the answer if the question asked for the first bedside imaging.
D. Plain X-ray gives no useful detail of an intraocular mass and adds radiation.
key_concept:
Leukocoria + squint in a young child = retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
  • Next step: urgent ophthalmology referral, dilated fundus exam under anaesthesia
  • Imaging of choice for extent: MRI orbits and brain
  • Ultrasound: shows calcification, no radiation
  • Avoid CT: radiation, second malignancy risk (RB1)
  • Other leukocoria cause: congenital cataract
exam_pearl: If "refer to ophthalmology" or "fundoscopy under anaesthesia" is offered, that beats any imaging choice.

stem: Scenario about baby with bronchiolitis symptoms, imaging of choice:
why_right: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in an infant with URTI symptoms followed by wheeze, crackles and tachypnea. When imaging is asked for, the chest X ray is the modality of choice: it shows hyperinflation (air trapping), peribronchial thickening and patchy atelectasis, and it is the test used if pneumonia or a foreign body needs excluding.
why_wrong_block:
B. MRI: no role in acute lower respiratory infection in an infant; slow, needs sedation, and adds nothing to management.
C. Ultrasound: lung ultrasound is a research or point of care tool, not the standard imaging for bronchiolitis; ultrasound is first line for things like intussusception or pyloric stenosis.
D. CT: high radiation and not indicated; reserved for complications or suspected structural lung disease, not a routine viral bronchiolitis.
key_concept:
Bronchiolitis = clinical diagnosis; imaging only if needed, and then CXR.
  • Cause: RSV most common
  • Picture: infant, coryza then wheeze, crackles, tachypnea, retractions
  • CXR (if done): hyperinflation, peribronchial cuffing, patchy atelectasis
  • CXR not routine; do it if pneumonia or foreign body suspected
  • Organism: nasopharyngeal aspirate
  • Treatment: supportive (oxygen, hydration)
exam_pearl: If the question asks whether imaging is routinely needed, the answer is no; if it asks which imaging, it is the chest X ray.

stem: TTN imaging feature?
why_right: Transient tachypnea of the newborn is caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, classically after a cesarean section at term. That retained fluid shows on chest X ray as fluid in the fissures (especially the horizontal fissure) with perihilar linear streaks and mild hyperinflation.
why_wrong_block: B. Basal infiltration: suggests pneumonia or aspiration (for example meconium aspiration gives patchy coarse infiltrates); it is not the TTN pattern.
key_concept:
Neonatal CXR patterns:
  • TTN: fluid in fissures, perihilar streaks, term CS baby, self resolving
  • RDS: diffuse ground glass (reticulogranular) with air bronchograms, preterm, surfactant deficiency
  • Meconium aspiration: patchy coarse infiltrates with hyperinflation
  • Pneumonia: focal or patchy consolidation
exam_pearl: Term + cesarean + fluid in the horizontal fissure = TTN; preterm + ground glass = RDS.

stem: 9 y/o boy with hx of URTI came with neck tenderness, his labs: Low TSH, Low T4, high ESR/CRP I think. Diagnosis?
why_right: The decisive clues are a recent URTI, neck tenderness and a high ESR/CRP with a suppressed TSH: this is subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis, a painful post viral thyroiditis. Inflammation releases stored hormone, so TSH falls; later the gland can pass through a hypothyroid phase before recovering.
why_wrong_block:
A. Graves disease: low TSH with high T4, but the gland is non tender, ESR is normal, and there may be eye signs or diffuse uptake; it does not follow a URTI with neck pain.
C. Hashimoto thyroiditis: painless goiter with high TSH (hypothyroidism) and positive anti TPO antibodies; inflammatory markers are not raised.
D. Euthyroid sick syndrome: abnormal TFTs (low T3 first, sometimes low T4 and TSH) in a child who is acutely, seriously ill, such as in ICU; it causes no neck tenderness or raised ESR.
key_concept:
Painful thyroid + recent URTI + high ESR = subacute thyroiditis.
  • Labs: low TSH, high T4/T3 in the thyrotoxic phase, high ESR/CRP
  • Radioactive iodine uptake: low (distinguishes from Graves)
  • Course: thyrotoxic, then possible hypothyroid phase, then recovery
  • Treatment: NSAIDs or steroids for pain, beta blocker for symptoms
  • Graves: diffuse high uptake, non tender
exam_pearl: Tenderness and high ESR beat the exact hormone numbers: a tender gland after a viral illness is subacute thyroiditis even if the recalled T4 looks off.

stem: Patient presents with swelling, the overlying skin was erythematous and fluctuance after a minor injury. What is the next step in management?
why_right: "Fluctuance" under erythematous skin after a minor injury means a collected abscess, not just cellulitis. Pus in a closed cavity is not penetrated well by antibiotics, so source control by incision and drainage is the treatment and the next step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics alone treat cellulitis (redness, warmth, no fluctuance); for an abscess they are only an adjunct after drainage when there is systemic illness, extensive surrounding cellulitis or immunosuppression.
C. A CBC does not change management of a localized abscess; it may help in a systemically unwell patient, but drainage is still needed.
key_concept:
Skin and soft tissue infection: is there pus?
  • Redness, warmth, no fluctuance: cellulitis, antibiotics
  • Fluctuant collection: incision and drainage
  • Breast abscess, small with healthy skin: needle aspiration
  • Crepitus, rapid spread, severe pain: necrotizing infection, surgical debridement
exam_pearl: No fluctuance = cellulitis = antibiotics; fluctuance = abscess = drain it.

stem: A 46-year-old man, whose father was recently diagnosed with prostate cancer, comes for advice on screening. On digital rectal examination, the prostate is smooth, regular, and the sulcus is palpable. What is the next best step in management?
highlight_terms_source: father was recently diagnosed with prostate cancer
smooth, regular, and the sulcus is palpable
key_concept:
Prostate screening start depends on risk.
  • Average risk: shared decision from about 50
  • First-degree relative diagnosed before 65, or Black: from about 45
  • Several relatives diagnosed young: earlier still
  • Screening test: PSA (DRE only as adjunct)
  • Abnormal DRE or raised PSA: further evaluation (MRI, biopsy)
exam_pearl: Same stem, different key: father diagnosed young or Black patient means PSA; father diagnosed old means reassurance.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler rule: If his father diagnosed before age of 65: B) PSA in 2 week. If father diagnosed after age of 65: A) reassurance. If he is Black: B) PSA in 2 week (regardless of family hx). Father's age not given in this recall, so no option marked. See 1356b/1356c variants (father 73 / 76: Reassurance).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 42-year-old male screened for prostate cancer. Father had prostate cancer at age 73. DRE mid? and soft. Most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: Father had prostate cancer at age 73
why_right: A 42-year-old with no symptoms and a soft prostate on DRE has no finding that needs work-up. His father was diagnosed at 73, i.e. after 65, so he does not count as a high-risk family history and he is below the usual age for average-risk screening discussion. Reassurance is therefore the most appropriate management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Immediate biopsy is reserved for an abnormal DRE (hard, nodular, asymmetric gland) or a raised PSA; this gland is soft and he has no PSA result.
C. Routine yearly DRE is not recommended as a screening tool in an average-risk man this young; screening, when chosen, is a shared decision based on PSA at an older age.
key_concept:
Prostate cancer screening depends on age and true risk, not on any family history.
  • Average risk: shared decision on PSA screening from about age 50 to 55
  • High risk (first-degree relative diagnosed before 65, or Black ethnicity): start earlier, around 40 to 45
  • Relative diagnosed after 65: treat as average risk
  • Hard or nodular DRE, or raised PSA: proceed to imaging and biopsy
exam_pearl: The age of the relative at diagnosis is the trap: a father diagnosed before 65 would change the answer toward early PSA screening.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's 'Q:' variant under 1356; options printed as A, B, D (third option lettered D in source). Father diagnosed after 65: reassurance.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the primary care clinic concerned about prostate cancer because his father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at the age of 76. The patient is completely asymptomatic with no urinary complaints. On digital rectal examination (DRE), the prostate is soft, smooth, of normal size, and the medial sulcus is easily palpable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at the age of 76
soft, smooth, of normal size, and the medial sulcus is easily palpable
why_right: This 45-year-old is completely asymptomatic and has a soft, smooth, normal-sized prostate with a preserved median sulcus, so the exam is normal. His father was diagnosed at 76, after age 65, which does not make him high risk. With no indication for testing, reassurance is the most appropriate next step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Annual DRE is not a recommended screening strategy and adds nothing for an average-risk man with a normal examination.
B. Transrectal ultrasound is used to guide biopsy or assess gland size, not to screen an asymptomatic man with a normal DRE.
D. PSA testing would be offered to a high-risk man at this age (relative diagnosed before 65) or to an average-risk man at an older age after shared decision making; neither applies here.
key_concept:
Normal DRE + no symptoms + relative diagnosed after 65 = average risk, reassure.
  • Abnormal DRE: hard, nodular, obliterated median sulcus
  • Early PSA screening only if first-degree relative diagnosed before 65 or other high-risk group
  • TRUS is a biopsy guide, not a screening test
exam_pearl: If the stem changes the father's age at diagnosis to under 65, PSA testing becomes the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's second 'Q:' variant under 1356.

stem: A father comes with his 3 years old daughter that missed (MMR, OPV, PCV, measles) due to travel and sickness. What to do at this visit? (Options exactly as in the exam, same order.)
OptA: Give polio vaccine only at this visit
OptB: start a catch up plan for vaccination
why_right: A child who has missed several vaccines should be brought up to date with a catch up schedule starting at this visit: give all due vaccines that can be given together and book the rest at the minimum intervals. The series is never restarted, travel or past illness is not a contraindication, and delay only prolongs the period of vulnerability.
why_wrong_block:
A. Give polio vaccine only: needlessly delays protection; multiple vaccines (including live MMR) can be given at the same visit, so MMR and PCV should not be held back.
C. Wait until school age: leaves a 3 year old unprotected against measles and pneumococcus for years; catch up starts now, not at school entry.
D. Vaccinations are useless nowadays: false and unprofessional; outbreaks of measles occur when coverage drops.
key_concept:
Missed vaccines = catch up now, do not restart.
  • Give all due vaccines at the same visit if possible
  • Live vaccines (MMR, varicella): same day or at least 4 weeks apart
  • MMR minimum age 12 months; dose 2 at least 4 weeks after dose 1
  • PCV and Hib not needed in healthy children 5 years or older
  • Minor illness and travel are not contraindications
exam_pearl: Any option that restarts the series, delays, or gives only one vaccine is wrong; the answer is catch up starting today.

stem: 6 Y/O boy brought by his mother c/o fatigue and O/E hepatosplenomegaly, labs showed WBC 2.5 Hb 8 also plt low. What is the next step to confirm the diagnosis?
why_right: A 6 year old with fatigue, hepatosplenomegaly and low WBC, Hb and platelets has pancytopenia with organomegaly, which points to marrow infiltration such as leukemia. The lead in is confirm the diagnosis, and only bone marrow examination (aspirate and biopsy) establishes it and classifies the disease.
why_wrong_block: B. Blood film: a quick supportive step that may show blasts, but it cannot confirm or classify leukemia and may be blast free (aleukemic); it would be the answer if the question asked for the initial test.
key_concept:
Two or more cell lines down = bone marrow.
  • Pancytopenia + hepatosplenomegaly or lymph nodes: think leukemia, confirm by bone marrow
  • Pancytopenia without organomegaly: think aplastic anemia, also bone marrow
  • Isolated low platelets after viral illness: ITP, marrow not needed (increased megakaryocytes if done)
exam_pearl: Initial test = CBC and film; confirmatory test = bone marrow examination.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0704B).
Compiler note: Compiler note: 2 cell lines defect: Bone Marrow Examination.

stem: 10yo boy with large swelling on the left side of his neck. On examination: 10 cm in size, soft and spongy. US FNA: clear lymphatic fluid. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: A soft, spongy lateral neck swelling in a child with clear lymphatic fluid on aspiration is a cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation). A 10 cm lesion will not regress and risks airway compression, infection and bleeding, so it needs active treatment. Of the listed options, surgical excision is the only definitive treatment.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation is acceptable only for small, asymptomatic lymphatic malformations; a 10 cm mass needs treatment.
C. Chemotherapy treats malignant neck masses such as lymphoma, which would give lymphoid cells on FNA rather than clear lymphatic fluid.
D. Radiotherapy has no role in a benign lymphatic malformation in a child and carries growth and malignancy risks.
key_concept:
Cystic hygroma = lateral, soft, transilluminant neck mass with clear lymphatic fluid.
  • Thyroglossal cyst: midline, moves with tongue protrusion, surgery (Sistrunk)
  • Branchial cyst: anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, cholesterol crystals
  • Cystic hygroma treatment: sclerotherapy, then surgery
exam_pearl: If sclerotherapy appears as an option it is usually preferred first for a macrocystic lesion; without it, surgery is the answer.

stem: A full term baby after CS developed tachypnea and low oxygen saturation, chest x-ray is shown, what is the diagnosis?
why_right: A full term baby born by cesarean section who develops tachypnea and mild desaturation soon after birth has transient tachypnea of the newborn. Without labor, fetal lung fluid is cleared slowly; the chest X ray shows fluid in the fissures and perihilar streaks, and it resolves with supportive care within days.
why_wrong_block: A. Diaphragmatic hernia: bowel loops in the chest with mediastinal shift, a scaphoid abdomen and absent breath sounds on one side, often known antenatally; it gives severe distress from birth, not a CS related wet lung.
key_concept:
Neonatal tachypnea by context:
  • Term + CS + fluid in fissures: TTN, self resolving
  • Preterm + ground glass, air bronchograms: RDS
  • Meconium stained liquor + patchy infiltrates: meconium aspiration
  • Scaphoid abdomen + bowel loops in chest: diaphragmatic hernia, insert NG tube, avoid bag mask
exam_pearl: Cesarean at term is the TTN keyword; prematurity flips it to RDS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall screenshots only. Another version on the same card: 'Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?' (CXR shown) with option A. Transient tachypnea of newborn (bold), and a handwritten note 'Q Egg shape'. Reference image: radiological findings in TTN (fluid in the horizontal fissure).

stem: Meningitis case about child who got all signs of meningitis, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered consciousness after URTI. What would you see in lumbar puncture? (100% this is almost all information you can get from the Qs)
OptA: Elevated leukocytes predominant neutrophils high protein, low glucose
OptB: Elevated leukocytes predominant lymphocytes normal protein, normal glucose
OptD: Elevated leukocytes predominant lymphocytes high protein, low glucose
why_right: This recall's key is viral meningitis: meningism appearing after a URTI in a child is read as a viral (for example enteroviral) meningitis, and viral CSF shows a raised white count with lymphocyte predominance, normal protein and normal glucose. Normal glucose is the single most useful feature separating viral from bacterial and TB meningitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neutrophils, high protein, low glucose: bacterial meningitis; it would be the answer with a toxic child, purpura, turbid CSF or organisms on Gram stain.
C. Normal leukocytes: makes meningitis unlikely; a child with neck stiffness, photophobia and altered consciousness is expected to have pleocytosis (a normal count with meningism suggests meningismus or very early disease).
D. Lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose: tuberculous (or fungal) meningitis, with a subacute course over weeks, TB exposure and cranial nerve palsies.
key_concept:
CSF by cause:
  • Bacterial: neutrophils, high protein, low glucose, turbid
  • Viral: lymphocytes, normal or mildly high protein, normal glucose
  • TB: lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose, subacute course
  • Glucose is the key fork: normal = viral
exam_pearl: Lymphocytes alone do not make it viral; lymphocytes with low glucose is TB.

stem: Diabetic patient come with lateral leg ulcer, warm leg and there is discharge and black base and pulseless in distal dorsalis. The most likely cause is:
why_right: This recall's key is venous, most likely reflecting the lateral leg location, the warm leg and the discharge (exudate), all of which fit venous ulceration. However, the stem also says pulseless dorsalis pedis and a black base, which are the textbook features of an arterial ulcer. The card is kept as keyed, but compare it with the near-identical recall where the pulse is intact.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neuropathic ulcers sit on pressure points of the sole (metatarsal heads, heel) in a warm foot with palpable pulses and loss of sensation, not on the lateral leg.
C. Malignancy (Marjolin ulcer) is suspected in a long-standing non-healing ulcer with rolled or everted edges; nothing here suggests it.
D. Arterial ulcers have absent pulses, a cold limb and a deep, punched-out, necrotic (black) base; the cold limb is missing here, but the absent pulse and black base point this way.
key_concept:
Leg ulcer: check the pulse first.
  • Absent pulse: arterial ulcer, arterial Doppler
  • Intact pulse: venous ulcer, venous duplex
  • Venous: gaiter area, shallow, irregular edge, pink granulating base, exudate, pigmentation
  • Arterial: pressure or trauma sites, punched out, deep, necrotic or sloughy base, cold limb
  • Neuropathic: plantar pressure points, painless, warm foot, pulses present
exam_pearl: In exam stems the distal pulse decides: absent = arterial, intact = venous.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Page marks Venous despite 'pulseless' in the stem (compare 1379, same options with intact pulse).

stem: 36 y/o male DM came complaining of ulcer in the medial site of the foot. WOTF is the highest risk of this ulcer?
highlight_terms_source: ulcer in the medial site of the foot
why_right: The key reads this as an ulcer over the medial aspect of the ankle/foot, the gaiter region, which is the classic site of venous ulceration. Venous ulcers result from sustained venous hypertension caused by valve incompetence, so venous hypertension is the strongest risk factor for an ulcer at this site. The patient is also young (36), making atherosclerotic disease less likely.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diabetes mainly causes neuropathic ulcers over plantar pressure points (metatarsal heads, heel) and contributes to arterial disease; it is not the main driver of a medial gaiter ulcer.
B. Atherosclerosis causes arterial ulcers on distal pressure or trauma sites (toes, heel, lateral malleolus) with absent pulses and pain, usually in older smokers.
key_concept:
Ulcer site points to the cause.
  • Medial malleolus / gaiter area: venous (venous hypertension)
  • Toes, heel, lateral malleolus, shin: arterial
  • Plantar metatarsal heads: neuropathic (diabetes)
exam_pearl: If the stem places the ulcer on the sole over a pressure point in a diabetic, the answer flips to diabetes (neuropathy).

stem: Diabetic patient come with lateral leg ulcer, warm leg and there is discharge and black base (in my exam there was sign of epithelization or something like that) and pulse is intact distal dorsalis (and another pulse also intact). The most likely cause is:
why_right: The deciding clue is the intact dorsalis pedis (and other distal pulses): a leg ulcer with intact pulses is treated as venous. A warm leg, discharge (exudate) and signs of epithelialisation also fit a venous ulcer. Even in a diabetic, intact pulses point to venous disease, and the next step would be venous duplex.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neuropathic ulcers occur over plantar pressure points with loss of sensation, not on the lateral leg.
C. Malignant change (Marjolin ulcer) is considered in a long-standing non-healing ulcer with rolled edges or rapid growth; epithelialisation argues against it.
D. Arterial ulcers require absent or reduced pulses and a cold limb; here the pulses are intact and the leg is warm.
key_concept:
Leg ulcer first step = check distal pulses.
  • Intact pulse: venous, venous duplex
  • Absent pulse: arterial, arterial Doppler / ABI
  • Diabetes does not override the pulse finding
exam_pearl: Same options with a pulseless foot would point to arterial; the pulse is the switch.

stem: 45 y old came with severe pain during and after defecation, along with bright red blood on toilet paper, on examination posterior midline tear in the anal canal with increased sphincter tone. Most appropriate initial treatment?
highlight_terms_source: severe pain during and after defecation
bright red blood on toilet paper
posterior midline tear in the anal canal
why_right: Severe pain during and after defecation, bright red blood on the paper and a posterior midline tear with increased sphincter tone are classic for an anal fissure. The lead-in is initial treatment, which is medical: stool softeners and fibre plus a topical agent that relaxes the internal sphincter (chemical sphincterotomy), such as topical nitroglycerin or diltiazem.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy is not needed for a typical midline fissure; it is indicated for atypical (lateral or multiple) fissures suggesting Crohn disease, or for red flags like age-related cancer risk.
C. Lateral internal sphincterotomy is for chronic fissures (over 6 weeks, sentinel tag) that fail medical therapy, not the initial step.
D. Antibiotics treat perianal abscess or infection (fever, fluctuant swelling, discharge), which is not present here.
key_concept:
Anal fissure: sharp pain on defecation + fresh blood + posterior midline tear.
  • All: fibre, fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths
  • Acute (under 6 weeks) or initial: topical nitrates or calcium channel blocker (diltiazem)
  • Refractory: botulinum toxin injection
  • Chronic failing medical therapy: lateral internal sphincterotomy
exam_pearl: Painless bleeding suggests hemorrhoids; painful bleeding with a midline tear is a fissure, and surgery only comes after medical failure.

stem: Pt post thyroid surg prez w numbness around lips and other hypocalcemia symptoms. Stated "Chovsteks sign". What's the cause?
key_concept:
Post-thyroidectomy complication by presentation.
  • Neck swelling + stridor within hours: hematoma, bedside wound exploration
  • Perioral numbness, spasm, Chvostek/Trousseau: hypocalcaemia, check calcium and replace
  • Hypocalcaemia refractory to replacement: check magnesium
  • Hoarseness, aspiration: recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Loss of high pitch: superior laryngeal nerve
exam_pearl: Chvostek and Trousseau signs mean calcium, not nerve injury, even though both follow thyroid surgery.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Child with wide complex tachy. Gave BP but I can't recall number but was low.
why_right: A wide complex tachycardia with low BP is unstable (presumed VT with a pulse), and any unstable tachyarrhythmia is treated with immediate synchronized cardioversion, with sedation if it does not delay the shock. Drugs are only for the stable patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. Adenosine: for stable regular narrow complex tachycardia (SVT) after vagal maneuvers; it may be considered in stable regular monomorphic wide complex tachycardia, never as treatment of an unstable one.
B. Amiodarone: the drug for stable wide complex tachycardia or after cardioversion; giving it to a hypotensive child delays definitive treatment.
key_concept:
Tachycardia with a pulse:
  • Unstable (hypotension, shock, altered consciousness, heart failure): synchronized cardioversion
  • Stable narrow, regular: vagal maneuvers, then adenosine
  • Stable wide: amiodarone or procainamide, expert advice; adenosine only if regular and monomorphic
  • Pulseless VT: defibrillation (unsynchronized), not cardioversion
exam_pearl: Check stability first; low BP makes the answer cardioversion regardless of QRS width.

stem: Patient in hypovolemic shock, what do you monitor?
why_right: In hypovolemic shock the best bedside marker of end-organ perfusion and adequacy of resuscitation is urine output, monitored hourly via a urinary catheter. It reflects renal perfusion and falls progressively with each class of hemorrhage, so a target urine output is used to guide fluid resuscitation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood pressure is maintained by compensation and only falls once about 30 to 40% of volume is lost, so a normal BP can hide ongoing hypoperfusion.
C. Heart rate is an early sign but is unreliable as a resuscitation endpoint: it is blunted by beta blockers, age or pacemakers and raised by pain or anxiety.
key_concept:
Resuscitation adequacy = organ perfusion, best tracked by hourly urine output.
  • Class I: urine output normal
  • Class II: tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure, BP normal, urine output mildly reduced
  • Class III: BP first drops, urine output markedly reduced
  • Class IV: urine output negligible
exam_pearl: BP is the last vital sign to fall in hemorrhage, so it is a poor monitor; urine output is the classic answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: In hypovolemic shock, the most reliable indicator of adequate tissue perfusion and resuscitation is urine output. (Recall marked B with '??'.)

stem: Pedo patient presented with abdominal pain and bloody stool what is the most likely cause
why_right: Bloody stool with abdominal pain means an invasive (inflammatory) colitis. Among the options only Campylobacter jejuni invades the mucosa and causes bloody diarrhea; it is one of the commonest bacterial causes of dysentery in children, often from undercooked poultry, and is treated with azithromycin when therapy is needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rotavirus: commonest cause of severe watery diarrhea with vomiting and dehydration in infants; stool is not bloody.
B. Norovirus: outbreaks of acute vomiting and watery diarrhea (schools, cruises); non bloody and short lived.
C. Cryptosporidium: watery, often prolonged diarrhea, especially from swimming pools or in immunocompromised patients; not bloody.
key_concept:
Bloody diarrhea = invasive organism.
  • Bacterial: Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella, EHEC (O157:H7, watch for HUS)
  • Parasitic: Entamoeba histolytica
  • Watery: rotavirus, norovirus, Cryptosporidium, Giardia, ETEC
  • Campylobacter: poultry; complications Guillain Barre, reactive arthritis; azithromycin

stem: Post total thyroidectomy (4 days) c/o of stridor and cough and SOB; upon inspection the nerve was damaged or stuck, I don't recall much. What's the management
why_right: This recall's key is cricothyroidotomy, read as the need for an immediate surgical airway in a patient with stridor and SOB after total thyroidectomy, where bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury leaves both cords near the midline and obstructs the airway. The source itself is debated: laryngoscopy is the step that confirms cord palsy, and tracheostomy is the definitive airway for persistent bilateral palsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tracheostomy is the definitive airway when bilateral cord palsy persists; it is a planned procedure rather than the crash airway, which is why the source split on it.
B. Laryngoscopy confirms vocal cord paralysis and is the answer when the lead-in asks for the initial or next diagnostic step in a stable patient.
D. Repair of the recurrent laryngeal nerve is done only when a transection is recognised during surgery; it is not the management of airway compromise days later.
key_concept:
Post-thyroidectomy stridor: match the timing and the lead-in.
  • Hours post-op + neck swelling: hematoma, open the wound at the bedside
  • Stridor from bilateral RLN palsy: secure airway (intubation), surgical airway if intubation fails
  • Confirm palsy: laryngoscopy
  • Persistent bilateral palsy: tracheostomy
  • Unilateral RLN injury: hoarseness, aspiration, usually no stridor
exam_pearl: Read the verb: diagnosis or next step = laryngoscopy; definitive airway = tracheostomy; emergency when intubation fails = cricothyroidotomy.

stem: Pt complains of bulge in his anus with fever, don't remember
why_right: The decisive clue is fever with a perianal bulge. A painful perianal swelling plus systemic signs of infection (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis) is a perianal abscess, which needs incision and drainage.
why_wrong_block: B. Thrombosed pile: a very painful, tender bluish swelling at the anal verge, usually after straining or constipation, and the patient is typically afebrile. Here the fever points to infection, not thrombosis.
key_concept:
Perianal swelling: fever or not decides.
  • Painful swelling + fever ± high WBC: perianal abscess, incision and drainage
  • Painful tender bluish swelling, afebrile: thrombosed external pile
  • Sharp pain with defecation, fresh blood, no swelling: anal fissure
  • Chronic discharging opening after an abscess burst: fistula in ano
exam_pearl: Remove the fever and the same painful perianal lump becomes a thrombosed pile.

stem: A Child with Kawasaki disease, already received IVIG and IV aspirin, his symptoms are still not improving, what will you do next?
highlight_terms_source: already received IVIG and IV aspirin
key_concept:
Refractory Kawasaki = persistent or recrudescent fever after initial IVIG plus aspirin.
  • No carditis: second IVIG, then infliximab, then tapering oral prednisolone, then pulse IV methylprednisolone
  • Carditis/coronary change: infliximab, then tapering oral prednisolone, then pulse IV methylprednisolone
  • Second IVIG is not first line once carditis is present
  • Echocardiography assesses the coronaries
  • Poor IVIG response predictors: high CRP, neutrophilia, low albumin, low sodium, high liver enzymes, age under 12 months
exam_pearl: Look for coronary dilation or carditis in the stem: it removes second IVIG from the top of the ladder.

stem: Child diagnosed with kawasaki disease, started on High dose Aspirin and IVIG, after 3 days, child was not responding, there was left coronary artery dilation. What is most appropriate treatment in this case?
why_right: The child is IVIG-refractory ("not responding" after high dose aspirin and IVIG) and already has coronary involvement ("left coronary artery dilation"). In that branch a second IVIG is not first line and rescue anti-inflammatory therapy is needed; among the options, IV methylprednisolone is the only rescue agent, so it is the key.
why_wrong_block:
B. Low dose aspirin is the antiplatelet maintenance phase once fever has settled (continued until coronaries are normal on echo); it does nothing to control ongoing vasculitis in a non-responder.
C. Oral oseltamivir treats influenza; it matters in Kawasaki only because influenza or varicella on aspirin carries Reye syndrome risk, not as treatment of refractory disease.
key_concept:
Refractory Kawasaki: decide by carditis.
  • No carditis: second IVIG first
  • Carditis or coronary dilation: infliximab, tapering oral prednisolone, pulse IV methylprednisolone
  • Aspirin: high dose in acute phase, low dose antiplatelet afterwards
  • Echo is the test to follow the coronaries
exam_pearl: If infliximab were listed it would compete with steroids in the carditis branch; with only these options, the steroid is the rescue.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant under 1419. Refractory Kawasaki with carditis present: infliximab, taper oral prednisolone, pulse IV methylprednisolone (second dose IVIG not first line when carditis present).

stem: A 4-year-old boy is diagnosed with Kawasaki Disease on day 8 of illness. He is admitted to the hospital for further management. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment regimen?
highlight_terms_source: Kawasaki Disease on day 8 of illness
why_right: This is a newly diagnosed Kawasaki disease ("day 8 of illness", asking for the initial regimen). Standard initial therapy is a single high dose IVIG infusion plus aspirin, ideally within the first 10 days of illness to reduce coronary aneurysm risk, so day 8 is still the ideal window.
why_wrong_block:
B. Aspirin with IV corticosteroid: steroids are an adjunct only in selected high-risk patients or a rescue for IVIG failure; they do not replace IVIG as initial therapy.
C. IVIG with cyclosporine: cyclosporine is a later-line option for disease refractory to IVIG and other rescues, not part of the first regimen.
D. Aspirin with infliximab: infliximab is a rescue for IVIG-refractory disease (especially with carditis), not the initial treatment.
key_concept:
Kawasaki initial treatment = IVIG plus aspirin.
  • Best given within 10 days of fever onset; still give after day 10 if fever or inflammation persists
  • Echocardiography at diagnosis and on follow-up
  • Refractory: second IVIG (no carditis) or infliximab/steroids
  • Cyclosporine: later rescue only
exam_pearl: "Initial" regimen always contains IVIG; any option with a biologic or immunosuppressant is a rescue line.

stem: Child 7 years old came for short stature, everything is normal but Delayed bone age and normal velocity. What you will do?
OptD: Reassure it will catch the adult height
why_right: "Everything is normal" with delayed bone age and normal growth velocity is constitutional delay of growth and puberty. These children have remaining growth potential, enter puberty late and reach a normal adult height, so the management is reassurance and growth monitoring.
why_wrong_block:
A. Changing dairy intake does not alter a normal variant; diet matters only when there is undernutrition with falling velocity or weight loss.
B. Basic labs (CBC, U&E and similar) are a screen for chronic disease when velocity is slow or the child is unwell; with a normal exam and normal velocity they add nothing here.
C. Increasing sun exposure targets vitamin D deficiency rickets, which would show bony signs and poor growth, not a healthy child with normal velocity.
key_concept:
Short stature with normal height velocity = normal variant.
  • Constitutional delay: bone age delayed, family history of late puberty, normal final height
  • Familial short stature: bone age = chronological age, ends short but on mid-parental target
  • Pathological: falling velocity, bone age delayed 2 years or more with low IGF-1 (think GH deficiency)
  • Mid-parental height best predicts final height
exam_pearl: Normal velocity is the reassurance clue; a falling velocity turns the same child into a workup.

stem: A 36-year-old patient presented with a neck mass that has been present for 3 years. Physical examination confirmed a palpable left thyroid gland; with no palpable cervical lymph nodes. Neck Ultrasound: Left thyroid nodule occupying most of the left lobe, measures 3.4 x 3.8 cm and has mixed cystic and solid components, the right lobe is normal. Fine Needle Aspiration: Finding is coded as Bethesda IV (suspicious for follicular neoplasm). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: FNA coded Bethesda IV (suspicious for follicular neoplasm) cannot separate follicular adenoma from carcinoma on cytology, because that needs capsular or vascular invasion seen on histology. The answer is a diagnostic lobectomy of the affected side: a left hemithyroidectomy, since the nodule is confined to the left lobe, the right lobe is normal and there are no nodes.
why_wrong_block:
A. Thyroid scan: used when TSH is low to look for a hot (autonomous) nodule before FNA. No suppressed TSH is given here and cytology is already available.
B. Total thyroidectomy: for Bethesda VI (malignant), medullary cancer, or bilateral disease. Here the disease is unilateral and not yet proven malignant, so removing the normal right lobe is overtreatment.
D. Repeat FNA: the step for Bethesda I (nondiagnostic) and Bethesda III. Repeating cytology for Bethesda IV will not resolve the question of invasion.
key_concept:
Bethesda category drives thyroid nodule management.
  • I nondiagnostic: repeat FNA
  • II benign: ultrasound follow up
  • III: repeat FNA
  • IV follicular neoplasm: hemithyroidectomy (lobectomy)
  • V: manage as IV or VI
  • VI malignant: (near) total thyroidectomy
exam_pearl: Follicular lesion on FNA means you need the capsule, so take the lobe; only Bethesda VI earns a total thyroidectomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recaller: not sure the recall was exactly this GB/MG one, but 100% sure it said Bethesda IV and asked for management.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with a groin swelling that appears when she stands and disappears when lying down. On examination, the swelling is located below and lateral to the Pubic Tubercle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: below and lateral to the Pubic Tubercle
key_concept:
Pubic tubercle rule for groin hernias.
  • Above and medial: inguinal (direct or indirect)
  • Below and lateral: femoral
  • Indirect vs direct: lateral vs medial to inferior epigastric vessels; deep ring occlusion controls indirect
  • Femoral: women, high strangulation risk, repair even if asymptomatic
exam_pearl: Women get inguinal hernias more often than femoral, so decide by the pubic tubercle, not by sex.

stem: Baby had a delayed separation of his umbilical cords and start bleeding from the site. Labs of coagulation normal PT, PTT and platelets count and function normal. There is delay in clot time only. Which factors is affected? I think clot lysis time was 5 seconds (I don't care, I choose F-13 anyway as all other options are wrong)
highlight_terms_source: delayed separation of his umbilical cords
normal PT, PTT and platelets count and function
why_right: Bleeding from the umbilical stump with normal PT, PTT, platelet count and platelet function points to factor XIII deficiency. Factor XIII cross-links fibrin to stabilise the clot; it acts after the cascade measured by PT and PTT, so routine tests are normal while the formed clot is unstable (screen: clot dissolves in urea solution).
why_wrong_block:
A. Factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A) prolongs the aPTT and classically bleeds into joints or after circumcision; here the PTT is normal.
B. Von Willebrand disease gives mucosal bleeding with abnormal platelet function testing and often a prolonged aPTT; platelet function here is normal.
D. Thrombocytopenia is excluded by a normal platelet count and causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding rather than stump bleeding.
key_concept:
Bleeding with ALL screening tests normal: think factor XIII deficiency.
  • Clues: umbilical stump bleeding, delayed wound bleeding, intracranial bleed in infancy
  • Test: clot solubility in urea
  • aPTT only prolonged: VIII, IX, XI (XII without bleeding)
  • PT only prolonged: VII
  • PT and aPTT prolonged: X, V, II, fibrinogen
exam_pearl: Delayed cord SEPARATION without bleeding, with infections and neutrophilia, is leukocyte adhesion deficiency, not a coagulation defect.

stem: Acute limb ischemia what is the risk for it?
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia: embolus vs thrombosis.
  • Embolic: AF, recent MI, valve disease; sudden onset, normal other limb; treat with embolectomy
  • Thrombotic: prior claudication or PAD (smoking, diabetes); acute on chronic; catheter directed thrombolysis
  • Features: 6 Ps (pain, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis)
exam_pearl: If the option list includes AF, that is the classic answer for embolic acute limb ischemia; claudication history points to thrombosis.

stem: Patient 2 months claudication pain, ABI was 0.3 CTA showed 3cm occlusion in popliteal artery, what's the most app step
key_concept:
Limb ischemia treatment fork.
  • Chronic claudication: exercise program, risk factor control, antiplatelet; revascularize if disabling or critical
  • Short focal lesion, viable limb: endovascular angioplasty or stenting
  • Long or diffuse lesion: surgical bypass
  • Acute embolic (AF): embolectomy
  • Acute thrombotic (on PAD): catheter directed thrombolysis
  • Nonviable limb: amputation
exam_pearl: Viability decides: a viable limb is revascularized, only a dead or unsalvageable limb is amputated.

stem: Old patient long history of leg claudication *for 2 months*, present with leg pain and ABI <0.3 and, *CTA show artery occlusion more than 3 cm* what to do?
why_right: This recall's key is amputation because the scenario is framed as acute on chronic ischemia: a long history of claudication, new leg pain, an ABI below 0.3 and an occlusion longer than 3 cm. The teaching rule used for this question is that acute on chronic ischemia with ABI below 0.3 (or an irreversibly paralysed limb) is managed by amputation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Thrombolysis: chosen for acute on chronic in situ thrombosis when the limb is still salvageable; here the severity markers in the stem (ABI below 0.3, long occlusion) are used to signal an unsalvageable limb.
C. Embolectomy: for embolic acute ischemia (AF, recent MI) in a previously normal artery; this patient has long standing atherosclerotic disease, not an embolic source.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia treatment by cause.
  • Cardiac embolus (AF): embolectomy
  • In situ thrombosis on PAD: catheter directed thrombolysis
  • Acute on chronic with ABI below 0.3 or irreversible paralysis: amputation
  • Initial step in all: heparin
exam_pearl: Embolus means embolectomy, thrombosis means thrombolysis, nonviable limb means amputation.

stem: Newborn with respiratory distress covered with meconum he was on conventional ventilation then high flow ventilation what most effective managment for him ?

Meconium aspiration not responding to ventilation = suspect PPHN.

stem: Picture of pediatric feet nails with koilonychia, the child presented with pallor, lethargy, and fatigue. CBC shows microcytic hypochromic RBC. What is the treatment?
why_right: Koilonychia (spoon nails) with pallor, lethargy and fatigue and a microcytic hypochromic CBC is iron deficiency anemia. The lead in asks for treatment, and the first line treatment of IDA in a child who can take tablets or syrup is oral ferrous sulfate. Response is checked by a rise in reticulocytes and hemoglobin after starting oral iron.
why_wrong_block:
A. Parenteral iron is reserved for failure of oral iron: malabsorption (e.g. celiac or IBD), true intolerance or persistent nonadherence. Nothing here suggests oral therapy has failed.
C. Folic acid deficiency gives a megaloblastic macrocytic anemia; this smear is microcytic and hypochromic.
D. B12 deficiency is also macrocytic and may bring neurological signs; it does not cause spoon nails or a microcytic picture.
key_concept:
Microcytic hypochromic anemia plus koilonychia = iron deficiency; treat with oral ferrous sulfate first.
  • IDA signs: pallor, fatigue, pica, koilonychia, angular cheilitis, glossitis
  • IDA labs: low ferritin, MCV, MCH; high TIBC, RDW, platelets
  • High RDW favors IDA; normal RDW favors thalassemia trait
  • No response to adequate oral iron: think thalassemia, so do Hb electrophoresis
  • Parenteral iron only when oral fails or cannot be absorbed
exam_pearl: Microcytic anemia not improving on oral iron: check adherence and dosing first, then think thalassemia trait (normal RDW, do Hb electrophoresis); it is not an automatic switch to IV iron.

stem: Picture of pediatric feet nails with koilonychia, the child presented with pallor, lethargy, and fatigue. CBC shows microcytic hypochromic RBC. What is the Diagnosis?
why_right: Koilonychia (spoon nails) with pallor, lethargy and fatigue and a microcytic hypochromic film is the classic picture of iron deficiency anemia, the commonest anemia in children. Confirm with low ferritin and serum iron with high TIBC.
why_wrong_block: B. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a MACROcytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils and possible neurological signs; it does not produce microcytosis or spoon nails.
key_concept:
Microcytic anemia: iron deficiency until proven otherwise.
  • IDA: low ferritin, low iron, high TIBC, high RDW, reactive thrombocytosis
  • Signs: koilonychia, pica, angular cheilitis, glossitis
  • Thalassemia trait: microcytosis with high RBC count, normal RDW, no response to iron
  • First line: oral ferrous sulfate
exam_pearl: Microcytosis that fails iron therapy with a high RBC count suggests thalassemia, not iron deficiency.
